“So please, let me stay here as your slave instead of the boy. Let the boy go back with his brothers. How can I possibly go back to my father if the boy isn’t with me? I can’t stand to watch my father die of a broken heart!”

Genesis.title: The Biggest Plot Twist: Joseph is Alive!
paragraphs: § The Big Reveal

Joseph just couldn’t keep it together anymore in front of all his staff. He yelled, “Everyone get out! I need the room!” So, it was just him and his brothers when he finally told them who he was. He was crying so hard that all the Egyptians heard it, and the news even got back to Pharaoh’s palace.
Joseph said to his brothers, “It’s me, Joseph. Is my dad really still alive?” But his brothers were totally shook. They couldn’t even speak; they were just staring, completely mind-blown.

“Come on, get closer,” Joseph said. So they did. “Yeah, it’s me. I’m your brother, Joseph. The one you sold to Egypt. But hey, don’t beat yourselves up about it. This was all God’s plan. He sent me here ahead of you guys to save lives. We’ve had this crazy famine for two years, and there are still five more to go, with no farming or anything. God sent me here to make sure our family line survives and to pull off this epic rescue mission. So, for real, it wasn’t you who sent me here. It was God. He made me like a father to Pharaoh, put me in charge of his whole house, and made me the ruler of all of Egypt.”
§ The Plan to Bring Jacob to Egypt

“Now, hurry back to my dad and tell him his son Joseph says: ‘God has made me the boss of all of Egypt. Get down here ASAP. You’ll live in Goshen, super close to me—you, your kids, your grandkids, all your animals, everything. I’ll take care of you. We’ve still got five years of this famine left, but I’ll make sure you and your whole crew have everything you need. You won’t lack a thing.’

“Look, you can see it with your own eyes, and my bro Benjamin sees it too—it’s really me telling you all this. Go tell my dad how I’m living large here in Egypt, tell him everything you’ve seen. But don’t waste time—get my dad down here now!”
Then Joseph hugged his brother Benjamin, and they both just cried. Then he kissed all his brothers and cried with them. After that, they finally started talking to him.
When the news hit Pharaoh’s palace that Joseph’s brothers were here, Pharaoh and his whole crew were actually pretty stoked about it.

Pharaoh told Joseph, “Tell your brothers the plan: Load up your animals, go back to Canaan, and bring your dad and your families back here. I’ll give you the best land in Egypt, and you’ll be living the good life.”

“And tell them this, too: ‘Take some wagons from Egypt for your kids and wives, and get your dad and come back. Don’t even worry about the stuff you’re leaving behind, because the best of everything in Egypt is yours for the taking.’”
§ The Journey Home

So that’s exactly what they did. Joseph gave them the wagons Pharaoh promised and a bunch of food for the road. He gave all his brothers brand-new clothes, but he hooked Benjamin up with 300 pieces of silver and a bunch of fresh outfits. And for his dad, he sent ten donkeys loaded with all the best stuff from Egypt, and another ten donkeys loaded with grain, bread, and other food for the trip back.
Then he sent his brothers on their way. As they were leaving, he told them, “Don’t get into any fights on the way back, okay? Just chill.”

They left Egypt and went back to their dad, Jacob, in Canaan. When they told him, “Joseph is alive! And he’s the ruler of all of Egypt!” he was just numb. He couldn’t believe it. But the more they told him everything Joseph had said, and when he saw the wagons Joseph had sent to bring him back, he started to come back to life. His spirit totally revived.
Israel said, “That’s all I needed to hear. My son Joseph is alive. I have to go see him before I die.”

Genesis.title: The Epic Family Road Trip to Egypt
paragraphs: So, Israel packed up everything he owned and started his journey. He got to Beersheba and took a moment to worship, offering sacrifices to the God of his father, Isaac.
That night, God spoke to Israel in a vision, calling out, “Jacob! Jacob!”
“Yeah?” he answered. “I’m listening.”

God said, “I am the God of your father. Don’t be scared about going down to Egypt. I’m going to turn you into a huge nation there. I’ll go down to Egypt with you, and I’ll also bring you back. And when you die, Joseph will be right there with you; he’ll be the one to close your eyes.”
§ The Big Move

So Jacob left Beersheba. Israel’s sons loaded up their father, their little kids, and their wives onto the wagons that Pharaoh had sent for him. They rolled into Egypt with all their livestock and the stuff they had gathered in Canaan. Jacob brought his entire family with him—sons and grandsons, daughters and granddaughters. Literally everyone.
§ The Whole Crew
Here’s the list of the Israelites, Jacob and his descendants, who went to Egypt:
Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn. Reuben’s sons were Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.
Simeon’s sons were Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jakin, Zohar, and Shaul, whose mom was a Canaanite woman.
Levi’s sons were Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.
Judah’s sons were Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez, and Zerah (though Er and Onan had already died back in Canaan). Perez’s sons were Hezron and Hamul.
Issachar’s sons were Tola, Puah, Jashub, and Shimron.
Zebulun’s sons were Sered, Elon, and Jahleel.
These were the sons Leah had with Jacob in Paddan Aram, plus his daughter Dinah. In total, that’s thirty-three sons and daughters.
Gad’s sons were Zephon, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli.
Asher’s sons were Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, and Beriah. They also had a sister, Serah. Beriah’s sons were Heber and Malkiel.
These sixteen were the children Jacob had with Zilpah, the servant Laban had given to his daughter Leah.

The sons of Jacob’s wife Rachel were Joseph and Benjamin. Joseph had two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, with his wife Asenath, who was the daughter of Potiphera, a priest of On. They were born in Egypt. Benjamin’s sons were Bela, Beker, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard.
These fourteen were the children Jacob had through Rachel.
Dan’s son was Hushim.
Naphtali’s sons were Jahziel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem.
These seven were the children Jacob had through Bilhah, the servant Laban had given to his daughter Rachel.

All in all, the number of people who went to Egypt with Jacob—his direct descendants, not counting his sons’ wives—was sixty-six. If you add the two sons born to Joseph in Egypt, Jacob’s family in Egypt totaled seventy people.
§ The Reunion

Jacob sent Judah ahead to get directions to Goshen from Joseph. When they arrived in the Goshen area, Joseph got his chariot ready and went to meet his father, Israel. The moment Joseph saw him, he threw his arms around his neck and just wept for a long time.
Israel said to Joseph, “I’m ready to die now. I’ve seen your face—you’re actually alive.”
§ The Game Plan

Joseph then talked to his brothers and his father’s family. “I’ll go and tell Pharaoh, ‘My brothers and my father’s family, who were living in Canaan, have come to me. These guys are shepherds; they’ve always raised livestock for a living. And they’ve brought their flocks, herds, and everything else they own.’ When Pharaoh calls you in and asks what you do for a living, tell him, ‘Your servants have always raised livestock, for as long as we can remember—us and our ancestors too.’ That way, he’ll let you settle in the Goshen area—because Egyptians really look down on shepherds.”

Genesis.title: Joseph's Family Moves to Egypt
paragraphs: § Family Reunion in Egypt
Joseph went straight to Pharaoh and was like, “My dad and brothers are here from Canaan! They brought all their animals and everything they own. They’re hanging out in Goshen for now.”
He brought five of his brothers to meet Pharaoh. Pharaoh asked them, “So, what do you guys do?”

They replied, “We’re shepherds, just like our ancestors. We came here because the famine in Canaan is insane, and there’s no grass for our flocks. If it’s cool with you, we’d love to settle in Goshen.”

Pharaoh looked at Joseph and said, “Awesome, your family’s here! Egypt is totally open to them. Let them live in Goshen, the best land we have. And hey, if any of them are really good at their job, put them in charge of my own livestock.”
Then, Joseph brought his dad, Jacob, to meet Pharaoh. Jacob gave Pharaoh a blessing, and Pharaoh asked him, “Dang, how old are you?”
Jacob said, “I’ve been wandering for 130 years. It’s been a tough life, and way shorter than my ancestors’ lives.” Then he blessed Pharaoh again and left.

Joseph got his family all set up in Egypt. They got the best land in the region of Rameses, just like Pharaoh ordered. Joseph made sure everyone, from his dad to the youngest kid, had everything they needed.
§ The Famine Gets Real

Eventually, the food ran out everywhere. The famine was no joke, and both Egypt and Canaan were struggling hard. Joseph collected all the money from people buying food and put it in Pharaoh’s treasury.
When everyone’s money was gone, the Egyptians came to Joseph, begging, “We need food! Are you just gonna let us die? We’re totally broke.”

Joseph was like, “Okay, if you’re out of cash, bring me your livestock. I’ll trade you food for them.” So, people brought their horses, sheep, cattle, and donkeys, and Joseph gave them food to get through the year.
§ Land for Food

The next year, they were back. “Sir, you know we’re broke. Our money is gone, and you have our animals. The only things we have left are our bodies and our land. Seriously, are you gonna watch us starve? Let’s make a deal. Take us and our land in exchange for food. We’ll be Pharaoh’s slaves, but at least give us some seeds so we can grow crops and not die.”
So, Joseph bought all the land in Egypt for Pharaoh. Every single Egyptian sold their land because the famine was that bad. Pharaoh ended up owning all the land, and the people became his slaves.
But Joseph didn’t buy the priests’ land. They got a regular allowance from Pharaoh, so they didn’t need to sell.

Then Joseph told the people, “Alright, listen up. I’ve bought you and your land for Pharaoh. Now, I’m giving you seeds to plant. When you harvest the crops, one-fifth of it goes to Pharaoh. You can keep the other four-fifths for yourselves, for seeds and for feeding your families.”
They were all like, “You’re a lifesaver! We’re actually happy to be Pharaoh’s slaves.”
Joseph made it a law in Egypt that a fifth of all produce belongs to Pharaoh. This law is still around today. Only the priests’ land wasn’t owned by Pharaoh.
§ Jacob's Final Request
So the Israelites settled in Goshen, got some property, and their population exploded. Jacob lived in Egypt for 17 years, making his grand total 147 years old.

When Jacob knew he was about to die, he called for Joseph. “Do me a solid. Swear to me you’ll be loyal and won’t bury me in Egypt. When I die, I want you to carry me out of Egypt and bury me with my ancestors.”
Joseph said, “I got you. I’ll do it.”
“Swear to me,” Jacob insisted. And Joseph swore.
Then, from his bed, Jacob bowed his head, grateful and at peace.

Genesis.title: A Grandfather's Blessing Gets a Plot Twist
paragraphs: A while later, Joseph got the news: "Your dad is sick." So he took his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, and went to see his father. When Jacob was told, "Your son Joseph is here to see you," he rallied and sat up in bed.
§ A Father's Declaration

Jacob said to Joseph, "The Strong God appeared to me at Luz in Canaan and blessed me. He told me, 'I'm going to make you have a huge family, a whole community of people, and I will give this land to your descendants as their permanent property.' Now, listen. Your two sons, who were born here in Egypt before I arrived, I'm adopting them. Ephraim and Manasseh will be my sons, just like Reuben and Simeon are. Any children you have after them will be yours, and they will inherit their property from their older brothers. I'm doing this for your mother, Rachel. It still breaks my heart that she died in the land of Canaan on our journey, just a short distance from Ephrath, which is now Bethlehem."
§ A Grandfather's Blessing
Just then, Jacob noticed Joseph's sons and asked, "Who are these boys?"
Joseph replied, "They are my sons, the ones God has given me in this place."

"Bring them to me so I can bless them," Jacob said. His eyesight was failing from old age, and he could barely see. Joseph brought his sons close, and Jacob kissed and embraced them. He said to Joseph, "I never thought I'd see your face again, and now God has let me see your children too!"

Joseph then moved his sons from Jacob's knees and bowed with his face to the ground. He took Ephraim in his right hand to place him at Jacob's left, and Manasseh in his left hand to place him at Jacob's right. But Jacob crossed his arms, placing his right hand on the head of Ephraim, the younger son, and his left hand on the head of Manasseh, the firstborn. Then he spoke this blessing:

"The God my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked with,
The God who has been my shepherd my entire life,
The Angel who has rescued me from all harm—
bless these boys.
May my name and the names of my fathers, Abraham and Isaac, live on through them.
And may they grow into a huge population on the earth."
§ An Unexpected Switch

When Joseph saw his father place his right hand on Ephraim's head, he was concerned he'd made a mistake. He took his father's hand to move it from Ephraim's head to Manasseh's. "No, Father," he said, "this one is the firstborn. Put your right hand on his head."

But his father refused. "I know, my son, I know," he said. "He will also become a people, and he will be great. But his younger brother will be even greater, and his descendants will become a multitude of nations." So he blessed them that day, saying, "In your names, Israel will speak a blessing: 'May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh.'" In this way, he put Ephraim ahead of Manasseh.
§ A Final Promise

Then Israel said to Joseph, "I am about to die, but God will be with you and will bring you back to the land of your fathers. And to you, as the first among your brothers, I give one more portion of land than your brothers—the portion I captured from the Amorites with my own sword and bow."

Genesis.title: Jacob's Final Words to His Sons
paragraphs:
§ Jacob's Last Words
Jacob got all his sons together and was like, “Yo, gather ‘round. I’m about to tell you what’s going to happen to you guys in the future.”
“Come close and listen up, sons of Jacob. Listen to your dad, Israel.”

§ Reuben
“Reuben, you’re my oldest, my first kid. You were supposed to be the strongest, the most honored, and the most powerful. But you messed up big time, like spilling a glass of water. You’re not on top anymore. Why? Because you hooked up with one of my wives, disrespecting me and my bed. That was a major fail.”

§ Simeon & Levi
“Simeon and Levi, you two are a real piece of work, always ready to throw down. I want nothing to do with your drama or your revenge plots. You guys kill people when you're mad and hurt animals just for fun. Seriously, a curse on your crazy anger. I'm gonna scatter your descendants all over Israel, like they're nothing.”

§ Judah
“Judah, you're the man. Your brothers are all gonna look up to you. You'll have your enemies in a chokehold while your own family bows down. You're like a young lion, coming back after a big win. Who would dare mess with a lion just chilling? A true king. The leadership will always belong to your family line. You'll be in charge until the ultimate ruler shows up, and everyone will follow him. You'll be so rich you'll tie your donkey to a fancy grapevine and wash your clothes in wine. Your eyes will be darker than wine, and your teeth whiter than milk. Total stud.”

§ Zebulun
“Zebulun, you'll set up camp by the sea. Your place will be a safe spot for ships, right next to the big city of Sidon.”

§ Issachar
“Issachar is like a super strong donkey just chilling between two saddlebags. He saw that his land was awesome and the country was beautiful, so he basically gave up his freedom to become a slave worker. Not the best trade-off, dude.”

§ Dan
“Dan will make sure his people get justice; he’ll totally hold his own among the tribes of Israel. But watch out, Dan is like a sneaky snake hiding in the grass. He'll strike a horse's heel and make its powerful rider fall flat on his face. Ouch.”

§ A Prayer
“God, I’m waiting and hoping for you to save us.”

§ Gad
“Gad is gonna get jumped by a bunch of raiders, but he’ll get them back in the end.”

§ Asher
“Asher’s crew will be known for making amazing food, like fancy desserts that are fit for a king.”

§ Naphtali
“Naphtali is like a deer running free, who has beautiful baby deer.”

§ Joseph
“Joseph is a total beast, like a wild donkey by a spring, full of energy. His enemies, those haters, came at him hard with their bows and arrows. But he didn't even flinch. He stood his ground, his bow ready, his arms strong, because he had the Champion of Jacob, the Shepherd, the Rock of Israel on his side. The God of your father will help you! The Almighty God will bless you with insane blessings—from the sky above and the earth below. Blessings of having lots of kids and livestock. My blessings for you are even bigger than the blessings of the ancient mountains or the epic hills. May all these blessings land on you, Joseph, because you were the one who stood out among your brothers.”

§ Benjamin
“Benjamin is like a starving wolf. He eats his prey all morning, and at night, he shares the leftovers.”

§ The End of an Era
These were the twelve tribes of Israel, and that’s what their father Jacob told them. He gave each of them a unique and personal blessing as his final goodbye.

Then he gave them instructions: “Look, I’m about to die. Bury me with my ancestors in the cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite. It’s the cave in the field of Machpelah, near Mamre in Canaan. Abraham bought that field as a burial plot. Abraham and Sarah are buried there, Isaac and Rebekah are buried there, and I buried Leah there too. The field and the cave were bought from the Hittites, so it’s legit.”
After Jacob finished telling his sons what to do, he pulled his feet up into bed, took his last breath, and passed away.

Genesis.title: Joseph's Final Act: Forgiveness and a Promise
paragraphs: Joseph just broke down. He threw himself on his father, cried his eyes out, and kissed him goodbye.
§ Saying Goodbye to Dad

Then, Joseph told the doctors who worked for him to get his dad’s body ready for burial, Egyptian-style. So they embalmed Jacob, which took the full 40 days. The whole country of Egypt mourned for him for 70 days straight.

When the official mourning time was over, Joseph went to Pharaoh's officials and said, “Hey, if you guys think I’m cool, could you do me a solid and pass this message to Pharaoh? My dad made me promise him something super serious. He said, ‘Look, I’m about to die. You have to bury me in the tomb I got ready for myself back in Canaan.’ So, can you please let me go and bury my dad? I’ll come right back, for real.”
Pharaoh was like, “Of course. Go bury your father, just like you promised him.”
§ The Long Road to Canaan

So Joseph headed out to bury his father. And it was a huge deal. All of Pharaoh’s top advisors, all the big shots in Egypt, they all went with him. Joseph’s whole family went too—his brothers and everyone. They just left their kids and their animals back in Goshen. They even had chariots and horsemen with them. It was a massive funeral procession, like something out of a movie.

When they got to the Atad Threshing Floor, which is just across the Jordan River, they stopped and had a huge mourning ceremony. It was super loud and went on for a while. For seven days, Joseph led these funeral rituals for his dad.

The local Canaanites saw all this intense grieving and were like, “Whoa, the Egyptians are mourning like crazy.” That’s actually how that place got its name: Abel Mizraim, which means “Egyptian Mourning.”

Jacob’s sons did exactly what their dad told them to do. They carried him into Canaan and buried him in the cave in the field of Machpelah, near Mamre. This was the same field Abraham had bought from Ephron the Hittite as a burial spot.
§ Brothers Get Scared

After the funeral, Joseph and his brothers and everyone who came with them went back to Egypt. But once they were back, his brothers started freaking out. They were talking to each other like, “Uh oh. What if Joseph is still holding a grudge? What if he decides to get us back for all the messed-up stuff we did to him?”

So they sent a message to Joseph that said, “Yo, before he died, our dad told us to tell you this: ‘Please, forgive your brothers for the terrible thing they did to you. It was really bad.’ So, will you? Can you forgive us? We’re all servants of the same God your father worshipped.”
When Joseph read their message, he started crying.
Then his brothers came to him in person, bowed down flat on the ground, and said, “We’ll be your slaves. For real.”
§ Joseph's Big Speech

But Joseph told them, “Chill out, guys. Don’t be scared. Do I look like God to you? Look, you totally planned to do something evil to me, but God flipped it and used your plan for something good. And the result is right in front of you—all these people are alive because of it. So seriously, don’t worry. You have nothing to be afraid of. I’ll take care of you and your kids.” He talked to them from the heart and made them feel a lot better.
§ The End of an Era

Joseph stayed in Egypt with his whole family and lived to be 110 years old. He got to see his great-grandkids from his son Ephraim. And the kids of his grandson Makir (from his other son Manasseh) were also considered part of his family.

When he knew his time was up, Joseph said to his brothers, “I’m about to die. But God is definitely going to come through for you. He’ll lead you out of this country and take you back to the land he promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.”
Then Joseph made them all swear an oath: “When God shows up to get you, you have to promise me you’ll take my bones with you when you leave.”
Joseph died when he was 110. They embalmed him and put him in a coffin in Egypt.

Exodus.title: Egypt's Got a Problem... and It's Us
paragraphs: Alright, so here's the deal. These are the names of the Israelites who rolled up to Egypt with Jacob, and they brought their whole crew:
Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah,
Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin,
Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher.
All in all, there were 70 people from Jacob's line. Joseph was already living in Egypt, you know?

Then Joseph died, and so did all his brothers—that whole generation passed away. But the Israelites? They were having babies like crazy. Seriously, it was a population explosion, and the whole land was filled with them.

A new king came to power in Egypt who had no idea who Joseph was. He was super freaked out and told his people, 'Yo, there are way too many of these Israelites. We can't handle this. We need a plan to keep them in check, or else if a war breaks out, they might team up with our enemies or just bounce and leave us hanging.'

So they forced them into work crews and made them do hard labor with these intense foremen. They built the storage cities of Pithom and Rameses for Pharaoh. But the crazier part is, the harder the Egyptians worked them, the more kids the Israelites had. There were kids everywhere! The Egyptians couldn't stand it and started treating them even worse, crushing them with slave labor. They made their lives a living nightmare with all the hard work—making bricks, mixing mortar, and doing back-breaking farm work. They just kept piling on the work, totally crushing them.

The king of Egypt then had a little chat with two of the Hebrew midwives, Shiphrah and Puah. He was like, 'When you're helping the Hebrew women give birth, check the baby's gender. If it's a boy, kill him. If it's a girl, let her live.'

But the midwives were seriously devout and had way too much respect for God to follow the king's orders. They let the baby boys live. So the king called them in and was like, 'Why did you disobey me? You let the babies live!'
The midwives told Pharaoh, 'Look, the Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women. They're super strong. By the time we even get there, they've already had the baby.'
God was actually really pleased with the midwives. And the people just kept growing in number and became super strong. And because the midwives honored God, He gave them their own families.
So Pharaoh just made a new rule for everyone: 'Every boy that's born, throw him in the Nile River. But let the girls live.'

Exodus.title: Moses's Wild Origin Story & Escape
paragraphs: So, check it out. This guy from the Levi family married a woman from the same tribe. She got pregnant and had a son. Right away, she could tell there was something super special about him, so she hid him for three months.

When she just couldn't keep him a secret anymore, she got a small papyrus basket, basically a little boat, and waterproofed it with tar. She put the baby inside and set it floating in the reeds along the edge of the Nile River.
The baby's big sister was watching from a distance to see what would go down.

Then, Pharaoh's daughter came down to the Nile to take a bath, while her maids were walking along the riverbank. She spotted the basket in the reeds and sent her maid to go get it. She opened it up and saw the baby—and he was crying! Her heart totally melted. She was like, "This has to be one of the Hebrew babies."
Just then, his sister popped up and asked her, "Hey, you want me to go find a Hebrew woman who can nurse the baby for you?"
Pharaoh's daughter said, "Yeah, go for it." So the girl went and got the baby's own mom.
Pharaoh's daughter told the mom, "Take this baby and nurse him for me, and I'll pay you." So the woman took her child and nursed him.
Once the kid was old enough, she brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, who adopted him as her own son. She named him Moses, which means 'Pulled-Out,' saying, "I pulled him out of the water."

Time went by, and Moses grew up. One day, he went out to see his own people, the Hebrews, and saw how hard their labor was. Then he saw an Egyptian beating up a Hebrew, one of his own relatives! He looked around, and when he saw no one was watching, he killed the Egyptian and buried him in the sand.
The next day, he went out again and saw two Hebrew men fighting. He said to the one who started it, "Yo, why are you hitting your friend?"
The guy snapped back, "Who made you our boss? You gonna kill me like you killed that Egyptian?"
That's when Moses freaked out. He thought, "Oh no, the word is out. People know."
Sure enough, Pharaoh heard about it and tried to kill Moses, but Moses managed to escape to the land of Midian. He sat down by a well.

Now, the priest of Midian had seven daughters. They came to the well to draw water for their father's sheep. But then some shepherds showed up and tried to chase the girls away. Moses stepped in, came to their rescue, and even helped them water their sheep.
When they got home to their dad, Reuel, he was surprised. "Wow, that was fast. How are you guys back so soon?"
They said, "Some Egyptian guy rescued us from the shepherds. He even drew water for us and watered the sheep!"
Their dad was like, "So where is he? Why'd you just leave him there? Go invite him to have dinner with us."

Moses ended up agreeing to live with the man, who then gave his daughter Zipporah to Moses as his wife. She had a son, and Moses named him Gershom, which means 'Sojourner,' because he said, "I'm a foreigner in a foreign land."
Many years later, the king of Egypt died. The Israelites were groaning under the weight of their slavery and cried out for help. Their cries reached God.
God heard their groaning.
God remembered his promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
God saw what was happening to the people of Israel.
And God understood. He got it.

Exodus.title: God's Crazy Job Offer from a Burning Bush
paragraphs: So, Moses was looking after the sheep for his father-in-law, Jethro, who was the priest of Midian. He led the flock way out to the west side of the desert and ended up at Horeb, the mountain of God. Out of nowhere, an angel of God appeared to him in a fire blazing from the middle of a bush. Moses looked, and for real, the bush was on fire but wasn't burning up.
Moses was like, “Whoa, what is going on? This is wild. For real, why isn’t that bush burning up?”
God saw him stop to check it out and called to him from the bush, “Moses! Moses!”
He answered, “Yeah? I’m right here!”
God said, “Don’t get any closer. Take off your sandals. You’re standing on holy ground.”
Then He said, “I am the God of your father: the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.”
Moses hid his face, lowkey scared to even look at God.

God said, “I’ve seen, like really seen, how much my people are suffering in Egypt. I’ve heard them crying out for help because of their slave masters; I know all about their pain. So now I’ve come down to rescue them, to pull them out of Egypt’s grip, and get them out of that country. I'm bringing them to a good land, a place with tons of space, a land flowing with milk and honey—the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites.

“The cry for help from the Israelites has reached me, and I’ve seen for myself how messed up the Egyptians are treating them. It’s time for you to go back. I’m sending you to Pharaoh to bring my people, the Israelites, out of Egypt.”
Moses said to God, “But why me? What makes you think I can just go to Pharaoh and lead the Israelites out of Egypt?”
“I’ll be with you,” God said. “And here’s the proof that I’m the one sending you: After you’ve brought my people out of Egypt, you all will worship God right here on this very mountain.”
Then Moses asked God, “Okay, but what if I go to the Israelites and say, ‘The God of your ancestors sent me,’ and they ask me, ‘What’s his name?’ What am I supposed to tell them?”
God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM. Tell the Israelites, ‘I AM sent me to you.’”

God kept going: “This is what you need to tell the Israelites: ‘God, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, sent me to you.’ This has always been my name, and this is how I’ll be known forever.

“Now get going. Gather the leaders of Israel and tell them, ‘God, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, appeared to me. He said, “I’ve seen what’s being done to you in Egypt, and I’ve decided to get you out of that terrible situation and take you to the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites—a land literally overflowing with milk and honey.”’

“Trust me, they’ll listen to you. Then you and the leaders of Israel will go to the king of Egypt and tell him: ‘God, the God of the Hebrews, met with us. Let us go on a three-day trip into the wilderness to worship our God.’

“I know the king of Egypt won’t let you go unless he’s forced to. So I’ll step in and hit Egypt where it hurts—for real, my miracles will have them spinning. After that, they’ll be happy to let you go. I’ll make sure the Egyptians give you a huge send-off. When you leave, you won’t be empty-handed! Every woman will ask her neighbor and any guests in her house for silver and gold things, jewelry, and extra clothes. You’ll put them on your sons and daughters. No cap, you’ll clean the Egyptians out!”

Exodus.title: Moses' Lame Excuses & God's Epic Comebacks
paragraphs: Moses was like, "Yo, they're not gonna trust me. They won't listen to a single thing I say. They'll just be like, 'God? Appeared to *him*? No way.'"
So God said, "What's that in your hand?"
"A staff."
"Throw it on the ground." He chucked it. It turned into a snake, and Moses legit jumped back, like, super fast!

God told Moses, "Reach out and grab it by the tail." He reached out, grabbed it, and boom—it was just his staff again. "This is so they'll actually believe that God, the God of their ancestors—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—appeared to you."
Then God said, "Put your hand inside your shirt." He slipped his hand in, then pulled it out. His hand was all messed up with leprosy, white as snow. Wild.
He said, "Put your hand back in your shirt." He did, then pulled it out again—totally fine, good as new.

"So, if they don't trust you or aren't convinced by the first sign, the second one should seal the deal. But if it doesn't, if they still don't trust you or listen to your message after these two signs, then grab some water from the Nile, pour it on the dry ground, and the water you pour will turn into blood the second it hits the dirt."
Moses hit God with another objection: "Master, please, I'm not a good speaker. I've never been good with words, not before you talked to me, and not now. I kinda stutter and get all tongue-tied."

God was like, "Uh, who do you think made the human mouth? And who decides if someone can't speak, or can't hear, or can see, or is blind? Isn't it me, God? So, get going. I'll be right there with you—and with your mouth! I'll literally teach you what to say."
But Moses said, "Oh, Master, please! Just send someone else!"

God got seriously angry with Moses: "Don't you have a brother, Aaron the Levite? I know for a fact he's good with words. He's a great speaker. Actually, right now, he's already on his way to meet you. He's gonna be so stoked to see you. You'll talk to him and tell him what to say. I'll be right there with both of you when you speak, teaching you every step. He'll be your spokesperson to the people. He'll be your mouthpiece, but you'll be the one calling the shots. Now take this staff in your hand; you're gonna use it to do the signs."
So Moses went back to his father-in-law Jethro and said, "I gotta go back to my family in Egypt. I need to see if they're even still alive."
Jethro said, "Go. Peace be with you."
God said to Moses in Midian: "Go. Head back to Egypt. All the guys who wanted to kill you are dead now."
So Moses put his wife and sons on a donkey and started the trip back to Egypt. He had a solid grip on that staff from God.

God told Moses, "When you get back to Egypt, get ready. All the miracles I'm gonna do through you, you'll perform them right in front of Pharaoh. But I'm gonna make him super stubborn, so he'll refuse to let the people go. Then you have to tell Pharaoh, 'This is God's message: Israel is my son, my firstborn! I told you to free my son so he can serve me. But you refused. So now I'm going to kill your son, your firstborn.'"

On the way back, when they stopped for the night, God met Moses and was about to kill him, but Zipporah grabbed a flint knife, circumcised her son, and touched Moses'... uh... private parts with it. She said, "Whoa! You're a bridegroom of blood to me!" Then God let him go. She said "bridegroom of blood" because of the circumcision thing.

God spoke to Aaron, "Go meet Moses in the wilderness." So he went, met him at the mountain of God, and gave him a hug. Moses told Aaron everything God had sent him to say and all the miracles he had commanded him to perform.

So Moses and Aaron went and gathered all the leaders of Israel. Aaron told them everything God had told Moses and did the miracles for everyone to see. And the people, they trusted it. They believed that God was actually concerned about what was happening to the Israelites and knew all about their suffering. They bowed down and worshiped.

Exodus.title: No Straw? New Problem: Pharaoh's Impossible Demand
paragraphs: So Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and said, “The God of Israel says, ‘Let my people go so they can have a festival for me in the desert.’”
Pharaoh was like, “Uh, who is this ‘God’ that I should listen to him and let Israel go? I don’t know any ‘God,’ and I’m definitely not letting Israel go.”
They replied, “The God of the Hebrews met with us. Please let us go on a three-day trip into the wilderness to worship our God. If we don’t, he might hit us with a plague or something deadly.”

But the king of Egypt said, “Moses and Aaron, why are you trying to get the people out of their work? Get back to it!” Pharaoh added, “Look, there are a ton of them, and you want them to take a break? Not happening.”

That same day, Pharaoh gave a new order to the slave masters and the foremen: “Stop giving the people straw to make bricks. Make them get it themselves. But they still have to make the same number of bricks as before. Don’t lower the quota at all. They’re just being lazy. That’s why they’re whining, ‘Let us go worship our God.’ Make them work harder. That’ll shut them up and make them forget about their God fantasies.”

So the slave masters and foremen went out and told the people, “Pharaoh’s orders: We’re not giving you straw anymore. Go find it yourselves, wherever you can. But you still have to make the same number of bricks every day.” So the people scattered all over Egypt looking for stubble to use as straw.
The slave masters were on their case, saying, “You have to complete your daily quota of bricks, just like when you were given straw.”
The Israelite foremen, who had been put in charge by Pharaoh’s slave masters, were beaten. They were asked, “Why haven’t you met your quota of bricks yesterday or today?”

The Israelite foremen went to Pharaoh and complained, “Why are you treating us like this? We’re not given any straw, but they keep telling us, ‘Make bricks!’ Now we’re getting beaten, and it’s not even our fault.”

Pharaoh shot back, “You’re lazy! That’s what you are! Lazy! That’s why you’re saying, ‘Let us go worship God.’ So get back to work. No one’s giving you any straw, but you better have your full quota of bricks at the end of the day.”
The Israelite foremen knew they were in a really bad spot when they were told, “You can’t make a single brick less than your daily quota.”

When they left Pharaoh, they ran into Moses and Aaron, who were waiting for them. The foremen told them, “May God see what you’ve done and judge you. You’ve made us look terrible to Pharaoh and his officials. You basically handed them a sword to kill us!”

Moses went back to God and said, “Lord, why are you being so harsh on this people? And why did you even send me? Ever since I went to Pharaoh to speak in your name, things have just gotten worse for them. And you haven’t rescued them at all. What’s up with that?”

Exodus.title: God's Ultimate Promise Drop
paragraphs: God told Moses, "Alright, now you're gonna see what I do to Pharaoh. I'm gonna hit him so hard he'll basically kick the Israelites out of his country."

God kept talking to Moses, telling him, "I am God. I appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as 'The Strong God,' but they didn't know me by my real name, Yahweh—the 'I-Am-Present' God. I made a solid promise with them to give them the land of Canaan, the place where they were just visitors. And now, I've heard the Israelites groaning because the Egyptians are still enslaving them, and I'm remembering my promise. So, go tell the Israelites this:

'I am God. I'm going to get you out from under the Egyptians' brutal slave labor. I'm going to rescue you from being their slaves. I'll buy you back, and I'll do it by throwing down some major judgments on them. I'll take you as my own people, and I'll be your God. You'll know for sure that I am God, your God who is getting you out of this mess in Egypt. I'll bring you into the land I swore to give Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and I'll give it to you as your own. I AM God.'"
But when Moses gave this message to the Israelites, they couldn't even process it. They were just so spiritually crushed and exhausted from the harsh slavery.
Then God said to Moses, "Go and tell Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, to let the Israelites leave his land."
Moses answered God, "Look, the Israelites won't even listen to me. How do you expect Pharaoh to? Besides, I'm not a great speaker—I stutter."
But God just laid out the facts again for Moses and Aaron about the whole situation with the Israelites and Pharaoh. And he commanded them again to lead the Israelites out of Egypt.
Here's the rundown of the tribe leaders:
The sons of Reuben, Israel's firstborn: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi—these are the Reubenite families.
The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jakin, Zohar, and Saul (whose mom was a Canaanite woman)—these are the Simeonite families.
These are the names of Levi's sons, in birth order: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Levi lived to be 137.
The sons of Gershon, by family: Libni and Shimei.
The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. Kohath lived to be 133.
The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi.
These are the families of Levi, according to their family lines.
Amram married his aunt Jochebed, and she had Aaron and Moses. Amram lived to be 137.
The sons of Izhar: Korah, Nepheg, and Zicri.
The sons of Uzziel: Mishael, Elzaphan, and Sithri.
Aaron married Elisheba, who was the daughter of Amminadab and the sister of Nahshon. She had Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
The sons of Korah: Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph. These are the Korahite families.
Aaron's son Eleazar married one of Putiel's daughters, and she had Phinehas.
These are the heads of the Levite families, listed family by family.

This is the same Aaron and Moses that God commanded, "Bring the Israelites out of Egypt, organized by their clans." These are the guys, Moses and Aaron, who told Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, to release the Israelites from Egypt.
And that was the situation when God spoke to Moses again in Egypt.
God said to Moses, "I am God. Tell Pharaoh, king of Egypt, everything I'm telling you."
And Moses just said, "Look at me. I'm a terrible speaker. Why would Pharaoh ever listen to me?"

Exodus.title: Pharaoh's Epic Fail: Snakes & Bloody Water
paragraphs: God told Moses, “Alright, listen up. I’m gonna make you seem like a god to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron will be your hype man. You say everything I tell you to, and Aaron will pass it on to Pharaoh. Then he’ll let the Israelites leave his country. But at the same time, I’m gonna make Pharaoh super stubborn, and then I'm gonna hit Egypt with some mind-blowing signs and wonders. Pharaoh’s not gonna listen to you, but I’ll show my power against Egypt and bring out my crew, my people the Israelites, from Egypt with some major acts of judgment. The Egyptians will know I’m the real deal when I step in and pull the Israelites right out of their country.”
So Moses and Aaron did exactly what God told them to. Quick fact check: Moses was 80 and Aaron was 83 when they went to talk to Pharaoh.

Then God said to Moses and Aaron, “When Pharaoh challenges you and says, ‘Prove yourselves. Do something amazing,’ you tell Aaron, ‘Take your staff and throw it down in front of Pharaoh. It’ll turn into a snake.’”
So Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and did just what God commanded. Aaron threw his staff down in front of Pharaoh and his officials, and it turned into a snake.

Pharaoh then called his own wise men and sorcerers. The Egyptian magicians did the same thing with their magic spells: each one threw down his staff, and they all turned into snakes. But then, Aaron’s staff totally swallowed their staffs. Wild.
But Pharaoh was still being stubborn and wouldn’t listen to them, just like God said he would.

God said to Moses: “Pharaoh is being a stubborn dude. He refuses to let the people go. First thing tomorrow, go meet Pharaoh when he goes down to the river. Stand on the bank of the Nile with the staff that turned into a snake and tell him, ‘God, the God of the Hebrews, sent me to you with this message: “Let my people go so they can worship me in the wilderness.” You haven’t listened so far. This is how you’ll know that I am God. I’m going to take this staff I’m holding and hit the Nile River water with it: The water will turn to blood; the fish in the Nile will die; the river will stink; and the Egyptians won’t be able to drink the water.’”

God told Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Take your staff and wave it over all the waters of Egypt—its rivers, canals, ponds, and all its pools—so they all turn to blood.’ There will be blood everywhere in Egypt, even in their pots and pans.”

Moses and Aaron did exactly what God commanded. Aaron lifted his staff and struck the water in the Nile while Pharaoh and his officials watched. All the water in the Nile turned to blood. The fish in the Nile died, and the river started to stink, so the Egyptians couldn’t drink its water. There was blood everywhere in Egypt.

But the Egyptian magicians did the same thing with their spells. So Pharaoh stayed stubborn. He wouldn’t listen to Moses and Aaron, just as God had said. He just turned and went home, not even giving it a second thought. But all the Egyptians had to dig new wells near the river for water because they couldn’t drink the water from the Nile.
A whole week went by after God struck the Nile.

Exodus.title: Pharaoh's Frog & Gnat Problem is Next Level
paragraphs: God told Moses, "Go hit up Pharaoh and tell him, 'God's message is this: Let my people go so they can worship me. If you refuse, I'm warning you, I'm about to drop a plague of frogs on the whole country. The Nile will be swarming with them—they'll get into your house, your bedroom, your bed, your staff's rooms, all over your people, even in your ovens and cooking pots. They'll be all over you, all over everyone—frogs literally everywhere, on and in everything. No cap.'"
God then said to Moses, "Tell Aaron, 'Wave your staff over the rivers, canals, and ponds. Bring up frogs all over the land of Egypt.'"
So Aaron stretched his staff over all the water in Egypt, and a whole mob of frogs came up and covered the country.
But then the magicians did the same thing with their magic tricks—they also made frogs appear in Egypt.
Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and was like, "Yo, pray to your God to get rid of these frogs. I'll let the people go so they can do their sacrifices and worship God."
Moses said to Pharaoh, "Bet. You name the time. When do you want the frogs gone from you, your servants, your people, and your houses? They'll be gone, except for the ones in the Nile."
"Make it tomorrow."

Moses said, "Tomorrow it is. This is so you'll know there's no one like our God. The frogs will be gone. You, your houses, your servants, and your people will be frog-free. The only ones left will be in the Nile."

Moses and Aaron bounced from Pharaoh's place, and Moses prayed to God about the frog situation he'd brought on Pharaoh. God came through on Moses' prayer: the frogs died off—in the houses, courtyards, fields, all gone. They piled them up in huge heaps, and the whole country smelled like dead frogs. It was nasty.
But when Pharaoh saw he had some breathing room, he got stubborn again and wouldn't listen to Moses and Aaron. Just like God said would happen.
God told Moses, "Tell Aaron, 'Take your staff and smack the dust. It's gonna turn into gnats all over Egypt.'"

And he did it. Aaron grabbed his staff, hit the dust, and it turned into gnats that were all over people and animals. All the dust in the whole country turned into gnats. Gnats were everywhere in Egypt.
The magicians tried to do the same thing with their spells, but this time they couldn't pull it off. There were just gnats everywhere, on people and animals.
The magicians told Pharaoh, "This is God's doing. This is legit." But Pharaoh was being stubborn and wouldn't listen. Just like God said.

God told Moses, "Get up early and go meet Pharaoh when he goes down to the water. Tell him, 'God's message is: Let my people go so they can worship me. If you don't, I'm gonna unleash swarms of flies on you, your servants, your people, and your homes. The houses of the Egyptians and even the ground they walk on will be thick with flies. But I'll make Goshen, where my people live, a safe zone—no flies there. That'll show you that I am God, right here in this land. I'll make a clear difference between your people and mine. This sign will happen tomorrow.'"
And God did exactly that. Thick swarms of flies filled Pharaoh's palace and his servants' houses. The whole country of Egypt was ruined by all the flies.
Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron in and said, "Fine, go ahead. Sacrifice to your God—but do it here in this country."

Moses was like, "That's not a good idea. The sacrifices we make to our God would seriously offend the Egyptians. If we do something they find that offensive right in front of them, they'll literally kill us. Let us go on a three-day trip into the wilderness to sacrifice to our God, just like he told us to."
Pharaoh said, "Alright, fine. I'll let you go sacrifice to your God in the wilderness. Just don't go too far. Now, pray for me."

Moses replied, "As soon as I leave, I'll pray to God that the flies will leave you, your servants, and your people by tomorrow. But don't play games with us again and change your mind about letting us go sacrifice to God."

Moses left Pharaoh and prayed to God. And God did what Moses asked. He got rid of all the flies from Pharaoh, his servants, and his people. Not a single fly was left. But Pharaoh got stubborn again and wouldn't let the people go.

Exodus.title: Pharaoh's Ego vs. God's Power: Hailstorm Edition
paragraphs: God told Moses, "Go to Pharaoh and tell him, 'God, the God of the Hebrews, is saying: Let my people go so they can worship me. If you refuse to let them go and keep holding them, I'm giving you a heads-up: God's gonna come down hard on your livestock in the fields—horses, donkeys, camels, cattle, sheep—hitting them with a serious disease. God will make a clear distinction between Israel's livestock and Egypt's. Not a single animal belonging to the Israelites will die.'"
Then God set the time: "Tomorrow, God's gonna do this."

And the next day, God did it. All of Egypt's livestock died, but not one of the Israelites' animals died. Pharaoh sent guys to check it out, and it was true: none of the Israelites' livestock had died—not a single one. But Pharaoh was still stubborn. He wouldn't let the people go.

God said to Moses and Aaron, "Grab handfuls of soot from a furnace, and have Moses throw it in the air right in front of Pharaoh. It'll turn into a fine dust all over Egypt and cause nasty sores and boils to break out on people and animals everywhere." So they took soot from a furnace, stood in front of Pharaoh, and Moses tossed it in the air. It caused boils to pop up on people and animals. The magicians couldn't even hang with Moses this time because of the boils—they were covered in them just like everyone else in Egypt.
God made Pharaoh even more stubborn. He wouldn't listen, just like God had told Moses would happen.

God told Moses, "Get up early and go to Pharaoh. Tell him, 'God, the God of the Hebrews, says: Let my people go so they can worship me. This time I'm about to hit you, your officials, and your people with my full power so you'll finally get it that there's no one like me in the whole world. You know I could've just hit you and your people with a deadly plague and wiped you off the map by now. But I've kept you around for one reason: to show you my power and to make my name famous everywhere. You're still acting all high and mighty at my people's expense and not letting them go. So here's the deal: around this time tomorrow, I'm sending a crazy hailstorm—the worst storm Egypt has ever seen since it was founded. So you better get your livestock inside—every person and animal left out in the open will die when the hail comes down.'"

All of Pharaoh's officials who actually respected God's word quickly got their workers and animals under cover. But the ones who didn't take God's word seriously just left their workers and animals out in the fields.
God told Moses: "Stretch your hands toward the sky. Signal the hail to fall all over Egypt—on people, animals, and all the crops in the fields."

Moses lifted his staff to the sky, and God sent thunder, hail, and crazy lightning strikes. God just rained hail down on Egypt. The hail was insane, mixed with lightning—a super intense hailstorm. There had never been anything like it in Egypt's entire history. The hail wrecked everything all over Egypt. Everything left out in the fields—people, animals, and crops—was destroyed. It even shattered the trees. The only place it didn't hail was in Goshen, where the Israelites lived.

Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron. He said, "Okay, for real, I've sinned this time. God is right, and I and my people are wrong. Pray to God. We've had enough of God's thunder and hail. I'll let you go. The faster you're out of here, the better."

Moses replied, "As soon as I leave the city, I'll stretch out my hands to God. The thunder will stop and the hail will end, so you'll know that this land belongs to God. But, I know you and your officials still don't actually respect God."
(The flax and barley crops were ruined because they were just about to be harvested, but the wheat and spelt were fine since they ripen later.)
Moses left Pharaoh and the city and stretched out his hands to God. The thunder and hail stopped, and the storm ended.

But when Pharaoh saw that the rain, hail, and thunder had stopped, he went right back to sinning, being as stubborn as ever, him and his officials. Pharaoh's heart became rock-hard. He refused to let the Israelites go, just as God had commanded through Moses.

Exodus.title: Egypt's Next-Level Disasters: Locusts & Total Blackout
paragraphs: So God tells Moses, "Aight, go see Pharaoh. I've made him and his crew extra stubborn, basically so I can show off these wild signs. This way, you can tell your kids and even your grandkids the story of how I totally messed with the Egyptians. For real, you'll have stories for days about the signs I dropped on them, and everyone will know I'm the one true God."

Moses and Aaron rolled up to Pharaoh and were like, "The God of the Hebrews has a message for you: How long are you gonna keep being so stubborn? Let my people go so they can worship me. If you don't, then get ready. Tomorrow, I'm sending a plague of locusts into your country. They're gonna cover everything, like, you won't even see the ground. They'll eat all the leftovers from the hail, even the new trees growing in the fields—total deforestation. Then they're gonna swarm your houses, your officials' houses, every single house in Egypt. It's gonna be a scene nobody, not even your great-great-grandparents, has ever witnessed."
Then he just turned and bounced, leaving Pharaoh shook.
Pharaoh's officials came to him like, "Bro, how long are you gonna let this guy mess with us? Just let the people go worship their God. Can't you see Egypt is literally falling apart?"
So they brought Moses and Aaron back to Pharaoh. He said to them, "Fine, go ahead. Go worship your God. But uh, who exactly is going?"
Moses was like, "Everyone. Young, old, our sons, our daughters, all our sheep and cattle—this is a huge worship festival for our God."

Pharaoh shot back, "Yeah, right. I'd sooner wish you Godspeed than let you take your kids. Look, I can see it on your faces, you're up to something shady. No deal. Just the men can go—go on and worship your God since you're so desperate." And with that, they got kicked out of Pharaoh's court.
God told Moses, "Stretch your hand over Egypt and give the signal. The locusts are coming to cover the whole country and eat every green thing the hail didn't destroy."
Moses stretched his staff out over the land. Then God sent this crazy east wind that blew all day and all night. By morning, the wind had brought a massive swarm of locusts.

The locusts swarmed the entire country of Egypt, landing on every single inch of it. It was thick with them. No cap, there had never been a locust invasion like this before, and there never will be again. The ground was just black with bugs. They ate everything—every blade of grass, every piece of fruit, anything the hail missed. All that was left were bare trees and empty fields. Not a single green thing could be seen in all of Egypt.

Pharaoh, totally panicking, called for Moses and Aaron ASAP. He said, "My bad, I've sinned against your God and you guys. Please, just forgive me one more time. Pray to your God to get me out of this mess—I'm literally dying here!"

Moses left Pharaoh and prayed to God. God switched up the wind, sending a super strong west wind that picked up all the locusts and chucked them into the Red Sea. Not a single locust was left in the whole country.
But God made Pharaoh stubborn again. He still wouldn't let the Israelites go.
Then God said to Moses, "Stretch your hand up to the sky. Let a darkness fall over Egypt—a darkness so thick you can actually feel it."

Moses stretched his hand to the sky, and a heavy darkness just blanketed all of Egypt for three days. No one could see anyone else. For three whole days, nobody could even move. But the Israelites? They had light right where they were living.
Pharaoh called Moses in and said, "Okay, for real this time. Go and worship your God. You can even take your kids. Just leave your flocks and herds here."

But Moses replied, "Nah, that's not gonna work. You have to let us take our animals for sacrifices and offerings to our God. All our livestock has to come with us, not a single hoof stays behind. They're part of how we worship our God, and we won't even know what we need until we get there."
But God kept Pharaoh's heart hard, and he refused to let them go.
Pharaoh yelled at Moses, "Get out of my face! And don't even think about coming back. I never want to see you again. If I ever see you again, you're dead."
Moses just said, "Fine by me. You'll never see my face again."

Exodus.title: The Final Plague is Coming
paragraphs: God told Moses, "Alright, I'm about to hit Pharaoh and Egypt with one last major blow, and after that, he's gonna let you all leave. For real, when he lets you go, he'll be so done with you guys, he'll basically be kicking you out."

"So, here's the plan. Tell everyone to ask their Egyptian neighbors for their silver and gold stuff." And God made sure the Egyptians were cool with the Israelites. Plus, Moses was basically a celebrity in Egypt; even Pharaoh's officials and the regular people thought he was a big deal.

Then Moses went right up to Pharaoh and was like, "Here's a message from God: 'Around midnight, I'm going to go through all of Egypt, and every firstborn son is going to die. From your son, Pharaoh, who's next in line for the throne, to the son of the servant girl grinding flour. Even the firstborn animals will die. There's going to be a massive outcry all over Egypt, like nothing you've ever heard before or will ever hear again. But for the Israelites? Not a single dog will bark at them. That's how you'll know God is making a serious distinction between Egypt and Israel.'"
"'Then all your officials will come to me, bowing down and begging me to get out of here, saying, "Please, just leave! You and all your people!" And you better believe I'll be out.'"
Moses was absolutely furious and stormed out from Pharaoh's presence.
God told Moses, "Pharaoh's not gonna listen to you, and that's lowkey the point. It's so I can show off even more of my power in Egypt."

So yeah, Moses and Aaron had pulled off all these insane signs right in front of Pharaoh, but God just made Pharaoh's heart even harder. And once again, he refused to let the Israelites leave the country.

Exodus.title: The Ultimate Escape Plan
paragraphs: So, God hits up Moses and Aaron in Egypt and is like, 'Yo, this month is now officially the start of your year.' He tells them to pass the message to all of Israel: 'On the tenth of this month, every family needs to get a lamb, one per house. If your fam is too small to finish a whole lamb, team up with a neighbor. Just make sure you have enough for everyone. And the lamb has to be a one-year-old male, no flaws, either a sheep or a goat. Keep it safe 'til the fourteenth, then the whole community of Israel will slaughter them at sunset. Then, you're gonna take some of the blood and paint it on the top and sides of the doorframes of the houses where you're eating. That night, you'll roast the meat over a fire and eat it with some flatbread (no yeast!) and bitter herbs. Don't eat it raw or boiled, make sure it's roasted—the whole thing, head, legs, and guts. And don't save any for breakfast; burn whatever's left.'
And check it, this is how you eat it: be ready to bounce, with your shoes on and your staff in your hand. Eat it quick, 'cause this is God's Passover.

'Tonight, I'm going on a walk through Egypt, and I'm taking out every firstborn, both people and animals. I'm also gonna wreck all the so-called gods of Egypt. I am the one true God. That blood on your houses? That's your signal. When I see the blood, I'll pass over you. No plague will hit you when I strike Egypt.'

'This day is gonna be a big deal for you guys. You'll celebrate it as a festival to God forever. It's a permanent thing. For seven days, you'll eat bread made without yeast. On day one, get all the yeast out of your houses. If anyone eats anything with yeast from day one to day seven, they're cut off from Israel. The first and seventh days are holy—no work. The only thing you can do is cook.'

'Keep the Festival of Unleavened Bread! This is the exact day I brought you out of Egypt in full force. Honor this day for all time. In the first month, from the evening of the fourteenth day to the evening of the twenty-first day, you'll eat unleavened bread. For those seven days, there should be zero yeast in your houses. Anyone, whether they're visiting or from here, who eats anything with yeast will be cut off from the community of Israel. Don't eat anything with yeast. Only unleavened bread.'

Moses got all the elders of Israel together and said, 'Go pick out a lamb for your families and slaughter the Passover lamb. Take a bunch of hyssop, dip it in the bowl of blood, and wipe it on the top and sides of your doorframes. Nobody leaves their house until morning. God's gonna pass through to strike down Egypt. When he sees the blood on your doorframes, he'll pass over your doorway. He won't let the destroyer come into your house and mess you up.'

'Remember this. It's a rule for you and your kids, forever. When you get to the land God promised you, keep doing this. And when your kids ask, 'Why are we doing this?' you tell them: 'It's the Passover sacrifice to God, who passed over the homes of the Israelites in Egypt when he struck Egypt but saved us.''
The people bowed down and worshiped.
The Israelites went and did exactly what God had commanded Moses and Aaron. They did it all.
At midnight, God struck down every firstborn in Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh on his throne to the firstborn of the prisoner in jail. The firstborn animals too.
Pharaoh and all his officials and everyone in Egypt woke up that night to some crazy loud crying. There wasn't a single house where someone wasn't dead.

Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron that same night and said, 'Get out of here! You and your Israelites! Go worship your God, whatever. And yeah, take your sheep and cattle like you wanted, but just go. And bless me too, I guess.'
The Egyptians were desperate to get them out, telling them to hurry up, saying, 'We're all gonna die!'

The people grabbed their dough before it could rise, wrapped up their mixing bowls in their clothes, and threw them over their shoulders. The Israelites had already done what Moses told them; they'd asked the Egyptians for silver and gold and clothes. God made the Egyptians like them, so they gave them whatever they asked for. Oh yeah, they totally cleaned out the Egyptians.

The Israelites traveled from Rameses to Succoth. There were about 600,000 men on foot, not counting their families. A mixed crowd of people went with them, plus huge flocks and herds of animals. They baked flat cakes with the dough they brought from Egypt; it hadn't risen because they were rushed out of Egypt and had no time to prep food.

The Israelites had lived in Egypt for 430 years. On the exact day the 430 years were up, God's entire army left Egypt. God stayed up all night, watching over the Israelites as he brought them out of Egypt. Because God kept watch, all of Israel for all time will honor God by keeping watch this night—a watchnight.
God said to Moses and Aaron, 'These are the rules for the Passover:'
'No foreigners can eat it.'
'Any slave who's been bought and circumcised can eat it.'
'No visitors or hired workers can eat it.'
'Eat it in one house—don't take the meat outside.'
'Don't break any of its bones.'
'The whole community of Israel has to be in on the meal.'

'If an immigrant is living with you and wants to celebrate God's Passover, all the males in his family have to be circumcised. Then he can join in and be treated like a native. But no uncircumcised person can eat it.'
'The same rule applies to everyone, whether you're a native or an immigrant living with you.'
All the Israelites did exactly what God commanded Moses and Aaron. That very day, God brought the Israelites out of Egypt, tribe by tribe.

Exodus.title: God's Ultimate Escape Plan & Road Rules
paragraphs: God hit up Moses and was like, “Yo, listen up. Every firstborn male, the first one out of the womb from the Israelites, whether it’s a person or an animal, is mine. Claimed.”

Moses then told the people, “Never forget this day. This is the day you bounced from Egypt, from the house of slavery. God brought you out with a seriously powerful hand. So, no eating bread made with yeast.

“You’re leaving during the spring month of Abib. And when God gets you to the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Hivites, and Jebusites—this awesome land flowing with milk and honey that he promised your ancestors he’d give you—you have to celebrate this service this same month.
“For seven days, you’ll eat bread without yeast. On the seventh day, there’s a huge festival for God.
“Yeah, for real, only yeast-free bread for seven days. Not even a crumb of anything fermented. No yeast allowed, anywhere.
“And on that day, you’ll tell your kid: ‘This is all because of what God did for me when I escaped from Egypt.’

“This whole observance will be like a sign on your hand, a reminder right between your eyes, and God’s teaching will be on your lips. Because it was with a powerful hand that God got you out of Egypt. You gotta follow these rules at the right time, every single year.

“When God brings you into the Canaanite land, just like he promised you and your ancestors, and hands it over to you, you have to set aside the first male born from every womb for God. Every firstborn male from your livestock also belongs to God. You can buy back a firstborn donkey by swapping it for a lamb. But if you don’t buy it back, you have to break its neck.

“You have to buy back every firstborn son you have. And when the time comes and your son asks, ‘Yo, what’s this all about?’ you tell him, ‘God brought us out of Egypt, out of slavery, with a crazy-strong hand. When Pharaoh was being super stubborn and wouldn’t let us go, God took out every firstborn in Egypt, both people and animals. That’s why I sacrifice every firstborn male animal to God and buy back every firstborn son.’ This whole thing is like a sign on your hand or a symbol on your forehead: God brought us out of Egypt with a powerful hand.”

So, it turned out that after Pharaoh finally let the people go, God didn’t lead them on the road through Philistine territory, even though that was the shortcut. God thought, “If the people have to deal with a war, they’ll probably freak out and just go back to Egypt.”
So God led the people the long way around, on the wilderness road toward the Red Sea. The Israelites left Egypt looking like a legit army.

Moses made sure to take Joseph’s bones with him. Joseph had made the Israelites swear a super serious oath, saying, “God will definitely come through for you, so you have to promise to take my bones with you from here.”

They packed up from Succoth and camped at Etham, right on the edge of the wilderness. God was out in front of them, leading the way in a Pillar of Cloud during the day, and at night, in a Pillar of Fire to light everything up. That way, they could travel day or night. The Pillar of Cloud by day and the Pillar of Fire by night never left its spot at the front of the people.

Exodus.title: The Ultimate Red Sea Escape
paragraphs: God hit up Moses and was like, “Yo, tell the Israelites to turn around and set up camp at Pi Hahiroth, right between Migdol and the sea. Make sure they camp on the shore, right across from Baal Zephon.

Pharaoh’s gonna think, ‘Lmao, the Israelites are totally lost and confused. The wilderness has them trapped.’ Then I’m gonna make Pharaoh’s heart all hard again, and he’ll come chasing after them. And I’m gonna use Pharaoh and his whole army to put my glory on full display. Then the Egyptians will finally realize that I am God.”
And that’s exactly what went down.

When the king of Egypt got the news that the people had bounced, he and his officials had a major change of heart. They were like, “What have we done? We just let our entire slave workforce walk free?” So he got his chariots all prepped and assembled his army. He took his six hundred best chariots, and all the other chariots in Egypt, with their drivers, came along for the ride.

God made Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, super stubborn, so he was dead-set on chasing the Israelites, who had just walked out on him without a single look back. The Egyptians went after them and caught up to them where they were camped by the sea—all of Pharaoh’s chariots, his horsemen, and all his soldiers, right there at Pi Hahiroth, opposite Baal Zephon.
As Pharaoh rolled up, the Israelites looked up and saw them—the Egyptians! Coming right at them!

They were totally freaking out. They cried out to God in pure terror. Then they started going off on Moses, “Bro, were there not enough cemeteries in Egypt that you had to drag us out here in the wilderness to die? What did you do to us, taking us out of Egypt? Didn't we tell you this would happen back in Egypt? Didn't we say, ‘Just leave us alone, we’re better off being slaves in Egypt than corpses in the wilderness!’”

Moses told the people, “Don’t be afraid. Stand firm and watch God do his thing and save you today. Take a good, long look at the Egyptians today, because you’re never gonna see them again, like, ever.
God will fight this battle for you. And you? You just need to shut up and stay quiet.”

God said to Moses, “Why are you crying out to me? Tell the Israelites to get moving. Hold your staff up high and stretch your hand out over the sea: Split it! The Israelites will walk right through the sea on dry ground.

“Meanwhile, I’ll make sure the Egyptians stay stubborn and keep chasing you. I’ll use Pharaoh and his entire army, his chariots and his horsemen, to show off my glory so that the Egyptians will finally get that I am God.”

The angel of God who had been leading Israel’s camp then moved and went behind them. The Pillar of Cloud that was in front of them also moved to the back. The Cloud was now between the Egyptian camp and the Israelite camp. It covered one camp in darkness but filled the other with light. The two camps didn't get near each other all night.
Then Moses stretched his hand out over the sea, and God sent a crazy strong east wind all night long that pushed the sea back. He turned the sea into dry ground. The waters of the sea split.

The Israelites walked through the sea on dry ground, with the water like a wall on their right and on their left. The Egyptians came after them in full-on pursuit, every single horse, chariot, and driver of Pharaoh’s army charged into the middle of the sea. It was the morning watch. God looked down from the Pillar of Fire and Cloud at the Egyptian army and threw them into a total panic. He messed up the wheels of their chariots so they were stuck in the mud.
The Egyptians said, “Run from Israel! God is fighting for them and against us!”
God said to Moses, “Stretch your hand out over the sea, and the waters will come crashing back down on the Egyptians, on their chariots, and on their horsemen.”

Moses stretched his hand out over the sea. As the sun came up and the Egyptians were trying to flee, the sea went back to its normal place. God basically yeeted the Egyptians into the middle of the sea. The waters came back and drowned the chariots and riders of Pharaoh’s army that had chased Israel into the sea. Not a single one of them made it out alive.

But the Israelites walked straight through the middle of the sea on dry ground, with the water forming a wall on their right and on their left. God saved Israel that day from the Egyptians. And Israel saw the dead Egyptians washed up on the seashore. They saw the incredible power that God used against the Egyptians. The people were in total awe of God and put their trust in him and in his servant Moses.

Exodus.title: God's Epic Victory Song & The Bitter Water Fix
paragraphs: Then Moses and the Israelites sang this awesome song to God, all of them together:

I’m shouting out my praise to God—He's so goated! He literally yeeted Pharaoh's horses and riders straight into the sea. God is my power, my favorite song, and for real, my ultimate rescue. This is my God, and I’m telling everyone about Him! He's the God of my ancestors, and I’m spreading the news everywhere. God is a total warrior, 100% God. He just dunked Pharaoh’s chariots and whole army into the sea. All his top officers? Drowned in the Red Sea. The ocean waves crashed over them; they sank like rocks to the bottom.

Your right hand, God, is crazy powerful; your right hand smashes the enemy. You're so majestic, you just crush anyone who tries to come against you. You unleash your anger and it’s like they’re toast. With just a breath from you, the waters piled up; the crazy streams literally stood up like a wall, and the wild ocean turned into a swamp.
The enemy was like, “I’m gonna chase them, I’m gonna catch them, I’ll take all their stuff, I’ll get my fill. I’ll pull out my sword, and my own strength will destroy them.”

But then you blew, and the sea just covered them. They sank like a lead weight in the massive waters. Who's like you among the gods, O God? Seriously, who compares to your power, your holiness, your amazing deeds, you miracle-working God?
You just stretched out your right hand, and the earth swallowed them. And the people you saved, you led them with your unfailing love; you guided them to your special place.

When other nations heard about it, they freaked out. The Philistines were shaking. The leaders of Edom were shook, and the big shots in Moab were terrified. Everyone in Canaan was panicking and just fainted. Pure dread and terror hit them. Your awesome power left them frozen like statues, until your people, the people you created, crossed over and entered the land. You brought them and planted them on your own mountain, the place you made to live, your sanctuary, Lord, that you built with your own hands. God will reign forever and ever!

Yeah, Pharaoh’s horses, his chariots, and his riders all went into the sea, and God made the water crash back down on them. But the Israelites? They walked right through the middle of the sea on dry ground. It was wild.
Then Miriam the prophetess, who was Aaron's sister, grabbed a tambourine, and all the women followed her, playing tambourines and dancing. Miriam sang this to them:
“Sing to God—what a victory! He pitched the horse and rider into the sea!”

After that, Moses led Israel from the Red Sea into the Desert of Shur. They traveled for three days in the desert but couldn't find any water. Then they got to a place called Marah, but the water there was bitter, so they couldn't drink it. That's why they named it Marah, which means "Bitter." And the people started complaining to Moses, like, “So, what are we supposed to drink now?”
So Moses cried out to God for help. God showed him a piece of wood. Moses threw it into the water, and the water became sweet and drinkable.
That was the place where God laid down some rules for them and started to test them.

God said, “If you really listen to me and do what I say, obeying my commands and following all my rules, then I won’t hit you with any of the diseases I sent on the Egyptians. Because I am God, your healer.”
Then they came to a place called Elim, where there were twelve springs and seventy palm trees. They set up camp there right by the water.

Exodus.title: God's Free Food Delivery in the Desert?!
paragraphs: So, on the fifteenth day of the second month after they bounced from Egypt, the entire Israelite community moved on from Elim to the Desert of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai. The whole community started complaining to Moses and Aaron right there in the wilderness. The Israelites said, “Seriously? Why didn’t God just let us die comfortably back in Egypt where we had lamb stew and all the bread we could handle? You’ve just brought us out into this desert to starve the whole community to death!”

God said to Moses, “I’m about to rain down bread from the sky for you. The people will go out and gather a day’s portion each day. I’m going to test them to see if they’ll actually live by my teachings or not. On the sixth day, when they prepare what they’ve gathered, it will turn out to be twice as much as their daily portion.”

Moses and Aaron told the People of Israel, “This evening you will know that it is God who brought you out of Egypt; and in the morning you will see the Glory of God. Yes, he’s heard your complaints against him. You haven’t been complaining against us, you know, but against God.”

Moses said, “Since it will be God who gives you meat for your meal in the evening and your fill of bread in the morning, it’s God who will have listened to your complaints against him. Who are we in all this? You haven’t been complaining to us—you’ve been complaining to God!”
Moses instructed Aaron: “Tell the whole community of Israel: ‘Come near to God. He’s heard your complaints.’”
When Aaron gave the instructions to the whole community of Israel, they turned to face the wilderness. And there it was: the Glory of God, visible in the Cloud.

God spoke to Moses, “I’ve listened to the complaints of the Israelites. Now tell them: ‘At dusk you will eat meat and at dawn you’ll eat your fill of bread; and you’ll realize that I am God, your God.’”

That evening, quail flew in and covered the camp, and in the morning there was a layer of dew all over the camp. When the layer of dew lifted, there on the wilderness ground was a fine, flaky something, as fine as frost on the ground. The Israelites took one look and said to one another, man-hu (What is it?). They had no idea what it was.
So Moses told them, “It’s the bread God has given you to eat. And these are God’s instructions: ‘Gather enough for each person, about two quarts per person; gather enough for everyone in your tent.’”

The People of Israel got to work and started gathering, some more, some less. But when they measured out what they had gathered, those who gathered more had no extra and those who gathered less weren’t short—each person had gathered as much as was needed.
Moses said to them, “Don’t leave any of it until morning.”
But they didn’t listen to Moses. A few of them kept some of it until morning. It got wormy and smelled bad. And Moses was furious with them.
