After Hazael was done with them, Jehoahaz's army was basically non-existent. All he had left were fifty cavalry, ten chariots, and ten thousand foot soldiers. The king of Aram had totally wrecked the rest, leaving pretty much nothing.

The rest of the story of Jehoahaz, all the stuff he did, it's all written down in *The Chronicles of the Kings of Israel*. Jehoahaz died and was buried with his ancestors in Samaria. His son Jehoash took over as king.

In the thirty-seventh year of King Joash of Judah, Jehoash son of Jehoahaz became king of Israel in Samaria, and he reigned for sixteen years. In God's eyes, he was also living an evil life. He didn't change a single thing from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who led Israel down the path of sin. He just kept on the same track, step by step.

The rest of the story of Jehoash, all his accomplishments and his war against King Amaziah of Judah, are written in *The Chronicles of the Kings of Israel*. Jehoash died and was with his ancestors. Jeroboam took his throne. Jehoash was buried in Samaria in the royal cemetery.

Elisha got super sick, and it was the sickness that he would end up dying from. King Jehoash of Israel went to visit him. When he saw Elisha, he just broke down and cried, saying, “My father, my father! The chariot and horsemen of Israel!”
Elisha told him, “Go get a bow and some arrows.” The king brought him the bow and arrows.
Then he told the king, “Put your hand on the bow.” He put his hand on it. Then Elisha put his own hand over the king's hand.
Elisha said, “Now open the east window.” He opened it.
Then he said, “Shoot!” And he shot.
“That's the arrow of God’s salvation!” Elisha exclaimed. “The arrow of deliverance from Aram! You're gonna fight Aram until there's nothing left of them.”
“Now pick up the other arrows,” said Elisha. He picked them up.
Then he said to the king of Israel, “Strike the ground.”
The king hit the ground three times and then just stopped.
The holy man got angry with him: “Dude, why didn't you hit the ground five or six times? Then you would've beaten Aram until they were completely done for. Now, you'll only defeat them three times.”
Then Elisha died and they buried him.

Some time later, some raiding bands of Moabites, like they usually did, invaded the country. One day, some guys were burying a man and they saw the raiders. They just chucked the body into Elisha’s tomb and ran for it. When the dead guy's body touched Elisha’s bones, the man came back to life, stood up, and just walked out on his own two feet. Wild.

Hazael king of Aram was a total pain and made life miserable for Israel during Jehoahaz's entire reign. But God was gracious and showed them mercy. He stuck with them because of His promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He never gave up on them, never even thought about ditching them, even to this day. Hazael king of Aram died. His son Ben-Hadad became the next king.

Jehoash son of Jehoahaz turned things around and took back the cities that Ben-Hadad son of Hazael had captured from his father Jehoahaz. Jehoash went to war three times and won each time, taking back the cities of Israel.

2 Kings.title: Kings Throwing Shade & Taking L's
paragraphs: Alright, so check it. In the second year of King Jehoash of Israel's reign, this dude Amaziah, son of Joash, took the throne in Judah. He was 25 when he started and ruled for 29 years in Jerusalem. His mom's name was Jehoaddin, and she was a Jerusalem local.

He was, like, mostly a good king who followed God. But, lowkey, he wasn't on the same level as his ancestor David. He was more like his own dad, Joash, and let all those sketchy local shrines stay open, where people were doing all sorts of wild stuff.

Once he had the kingdom on lock, he had the guards who assassinated his father executed. But he didn't kill their sons, which was actually pretty cool of him. He was following what God said in the law of Moses: parents don't pay for their kids' sins, and kids don't pay for their parents'. You're responsible for your own mess, you know?
Amaziah had this massive victory against Edom in the Valley of Salt, like, 10,000 casualties. He also conquered a city called The Rock and renamed it Joktheel, which is what it's still called.
But then he got a big head and challenged Jehoash, the king of Israel, to a fight. He was like, "Yo, come at me. Let's settle this face-to-face."

Jehoash's reply was savage. He basically told him a story about a little thistle that tried to marry a giant cedar tree's daughter, but then a wild animal just stepped on it and crushed it. He was saying, "Dude, just because you beat Edom, you think you're a big deal? Be proud, but stay in your lane. Why risk getting wrecked and taking Judah down with you?"
But Amaziah wouldn't listen. So, Jehoash, the king of Israel, went to battle against him at Beth Shemesh in Judah.
And, yeah, Judah got completely owned by Israel. All their soldiers just ran home.

Jehoash of Israel captured Amaziah of Judah right there. But he didn't stop. He went on to Jerusalem and tore down a huge chunk of the city wall, like 600 feet of it. He looted everything valuable from the temple and the palace—gold, silver, all of it. He even took hostages before heading back to Samaria.

The rest of the story about Jehoash, all his accomplishments, and the beef with Amaziah, is written down in the official records of Israel's kings. Then he died and was buried in Samaria with the other kings, and his son Jeroboam took over.
Amaziah, the king of Judah, actually outlived Jehoash of Israel by 15 years. The rest of his life is in the history books of Judah's kings.

Eventually, some people in Jerusalem plotted against Amaziah, and he had to run to a town called Lachish. But they hunted him down and killed him there. They brought his body back on a horse and buried him in Jerusalem with his ancestors.
Then the people of Judah made his son, Azariah, the new king. He was only 16! After his dad died, he rebuilt and restored the town of Elath to Judah.

Meanwhile, back in the 15th year of King Amaziah of Judah, Jeroboam son of Jehoash became the king of Israel in Samaria. He ruled for 41 years. And honestly? He was a pretty bad king in God's eyes. He just kept doing all the same sinful stuff that the first Jeroboam did, leading Israel down the wrong path. But, he did manage to get back some of Israel's old territory, from Lebo Hamath all the way to the Dead Sea. This was actually what God had predicted through the prophet Jonah.

See, God knew how much Israel was struggling. Times were tough for everyone, and there was no help in sight. But God wasn't ready to just erase Israel from the map. So he used Jeroboam, even though he was a bad king, to save them.

The rest of Jeroboam's story, his wins in battle, and how he got back Damascus and Hamath for Israel, that's all in the history books too. Then Jeroboam died and was buried, and his son Zechariah became the next king.

2 Kings.title: Israel's Royal Rumble: Kings Keep Getting Axed
paragraphs: Yo, so in the 27th year that Jeroboam was king of Israel, this guy Azariah, son of Amaziah, became king in Judah. He was only 16 when he started and ended up ruling for a wild 52 years in Jerusalem. His mom was Jecoliah from Jerusalem. He was actually pretty decent in God's eyes, kinda following his dad Amaziah's lead. But, plot twist, he didn't tear down the local shrines where people were doing all sorts of sketchy religious stuff; those places stayed super popular.

Then God hit the king with a nasty skin disease that stuck with him until he died. He had to live in a separate house and couldn't really be king anymore. His son Jotham stepped up to run the government and rule the country for him.

The rest of the story of Azariah, all the stuff he did, is written down in the official records of the kings of Judah. Azariah eventually died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David, and his son Jotham took over as king.

In the 38th year of Azariah's rule in Judah, Zechariah, son of Jeroboam, became king over Israel in Samaria. But dude only lasted for six months. He was a total mess in God's eyes, just like his ancestors. He kept up the same messed-up traditions of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who got Israel hooked on sin in the first place.
Then this guy Shallum son of Jabesh plotted against him and straight-up assassinated him in front of everyone. Shallum then took over as king.

The rest of Zechariah's short and messy life is all written down in the official records of the kings of Israel. This was basically God's word coming true, the one he gave to Jehu saying, "Your family will rule Israel for four generations." Zechariah was the fourth one. The end.
Shallum son of Jabesh became king in the 39th year of King Azariah of Judah. He was king in Samaria for... wait for it... just one month.
Then Menahem son of Gadi rolled up from Tirzah to Samaria, attacked Shallum, and killed him. Then he made himself king.
The rest of Shallum's one-month-reign and the whole conspiracy story are written in the official records of the kings of Israel.

Menahem, now king, started his reign from Tirzah by absolutely wrecking the town of Tiphsah and its suburbs just because they didn't welcome him. It got super dark—he brutally killed all the pregnant women there.

In the 39th year of King Azariah of Judah, Menahem son of Gadi became king over Israel. He ruled from Samaria for ten years. And yeah, he was another evil one in God's book. He just copied all the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who got Israel into that whole sin lifestyle.

Then the king of Assyria, Tiglath-Pileser III, showed up and invaded. But Menahem cut a deal with him. He basically bought the Assyrian king's support by giving him 37 tons of silver. He got the cash by taxing every rich landowner in Israel 50 shekels each for the Assyrian king. That made the king of Assyria happy, and he bounced.
The rest of Menahem's life and all his deeds are in the official records of the kings of Israel. Menahem died and was buried, and his son Pekahiah became the next king.

In the 50th year of King Azariah of Judah, Pekahiah son of Menahem became king of Israel. He ruled in Samaria for two years. And you guessed it—he was evil in God's eyes. He stayed on the same old sinful path of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who led Israel down the wrong road.

But then his own military aide, Pekah son of Remaliah, conspired against him. He straight-up murdered him in his own private room in the palace in Samaria. He also killed two other guys, Argob and Arieh. Fifty men from Gilead were in on the plot with him. After the murder, Pekah became the new king.
The rest of Pekahiah's life and everything he did is written in the official records of the kings of Israel.

In the 52nd year of King Azariah of Judah, Pekah son of Remaliah became king of Israel in Samaria. He ruled for twenty years. From God's perspective, he was a bad dude. He didn't change a single thing from the sinful path that Jeroboam son of Nebat had started, the one that got Israel sinning.

During Pekah's reign, the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser III invaded again. He captured a bunch of towns—Ijon, Abel Beth Maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee, basically the whole region of Naphtali—and deported everyone to Assyria.
But then Hoshea son of Elah started a conspiracy against Pekah. He assassinated him and took over as king. This all happened in the 20th year of Jotham, son of Uzziah's, reign.
The rest of Pekah's story and everything he did is written in the official records of the kings of Israel.

In the second year of Pekah's reign in Israel, Jotham son of Uzziah became king of Judah. He was 25 when he started and ruled for 16 years in Jerusalem. His mom was Jerusha, daughter of Zadok. He was actually a good king in God's eyes, following his dad Uzziah's example. But he also didn't get rid of the local shrines, and they stayed as popular as ever. He was the one who had the High Gate of God's Temple built.

The rest of Jotham's life and all his accomplishments are written in the official records of the kings of Judah. It was during his time that God started sending King Rezin of Aram and King Pekah of Israel to attack Judah. Jotham eventually died and was buried in his family's tomb in the City of David. His son Ahaz became the next king.

2 Kings.title: King Ahaz's Epic Fail & His Knock-Off Altar
paragraphs: So, in the seventeenth year of King Pekah of Israel, Ahaz, who was Jotham's son, became the king of Judah. He was twenty when he started his reign, and he ruled in Jerusalem for sixteen years. But get this—he wasn't living right in God's eyes; he was nothing like his ancestor David. He basically copied the playbook of the kings of Israel and even did some seriously messed-up stuff, like sacrificing his own son in a fire ritual. Total pagan move he picked up from the nations God had kicked out of the land earlier. He was also all about those sketchy local shrines for sex and religion that were popping up everywhere.
Then, King Rezin of Aram and King Pekah of Israel teamed up to attack Jerusalem. They put the city under siege, but they couldn't actually break through and get to Ahaz.
Around the same time, on another front, the king of Edom took back the port of Elath and kicked out the people of Judah. The Edomites moved in and have been there ever since.

Ahaz was freaking out, so he sent a message to King Tiglath-Pileser of Assyria, saying, "Yo, I'm your guy, your servant. You gotta come save me from the king of Aram and the king of Israel. They're crushing me right now." Then Ahaz totally looted the treasuries of the palace and God's Temple, grabbing all the gold and silver to send to the Assyrian king as a bribe.
The Assyrian king was like, "Aight, bet." He went and attacked Damascus, captured it, and deported all the people to Nineveh as exiles. And as for King Rezin? He had him killed.

Later, King Ahaz went to Damascus to meet up with King Tiglath-Pileser. While he was there, he was super impressed by this altar. He sent a sketch and a full set of blueprints for it back to Uriah the priest. So, Uriah the priest built an identical altar based on the plans Ahaz sent. By the time the king got back from Damascus, the new altar was ready.

The second the king saw the new altar, he went up to it and started a whole worship service. He did all the offerings: Whole-Burnt-Offerings with tons of smoke, Grain-Offerings, Drink-Offerings, and even sprinkled blood from the Peace-Offerings—the whole nine yards. But the original bronze Altar, the one that represented God's presence, he just shoved it aside to make room for his new, fancy one.

Then King Ahaz told Uriah the priest, "From now on, do all the sacrifices on this new, great altar. The morning burnt offerings, the evening grain offerings, the king's offerings, the people's offerings, all of it. Splash all the blood against this altar. The old bronze one? I'll just use that for my own personal stuff."
And Uriah the priest did exactly what King Ahaz told him to do.

Then King Ahaz went on a spree, stripping all the bronze from the Temple's furniture. He even took the four bronze oxen that held up the giant basin, called The Sea, and just plopped The Sea on the stone floor. To top it off, he got rid of any special features in the Temple that he thought might offend the king of Assyria.

If you want the rest of the tea on Ahaz and everything he did, it's all written down in The Chronicles of the Kings of Judah. Ahaz eventually died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David, and his son Hezekiah took over as the next king.

2 Kings.title: Israel Gets DEPORTED?! The OG Cancel Culture
paragraphs: So, in the 12th year that Ahaz was king of Judah, this dude Hoshea, son of Elah, became the king of Israel. He ruled from Samaria for nine years. And from God's POV, he was living a pretty bad life, but honestly, not as bad as the kings that came before him.

Then, Shalmaneser, the king of Assyria, rolled up and attacked. Hoshea was basically already his puppet and had to send him money regularly. But Shalmaneser found out Hoshea was being a total snake behind his back, trying to make a deal with King So of Egypt. And to make it worse, Hoshea was super late on his payments to Assyria. So, the Assyrian king had him arrested and thrown in jail. After that, he just invaded the whole country. He went after Samaria and laid siege to it for three whole years.

In the ninth year of Hoshea's rule, the king of Assyria finally took over Samaria and kicked the Israelites out, sending them into exile in Assyria. He moved them to Halah, to Gozan on the Habor River, and to the towns of the Medes.

This whole exile thing happened because of sin. The people of Israel sinned against their God, the same God who saved them from Egypt and the tyranny of the Pharaoh. They started worshipping other gods, copying the lifestyles of the pagan nations God had already kicked out, and just went along with whatever their own kings wanted. They were doing all sorts of shady stuff against their God, and then they weren't even hiding it anymore, building these gross sex-and-religion shrines all over the place. They put up their weird symbols at basically every corner. Everywhere you looked, they were making offerings to fake gods—the same exact stuff that got the other nations exiled in the first place. They racked up a huge list of evil deeds, and God was just completely over it, especially their obsession with worshipping idols made of wood and clay, even though He had clearly told them, "Don't do this—ever!"

God had warned Israel and Judah, sending a ton of prophets and seers over and over again to tell them, "Yo, turn away from your evil lifestyle. Just do what I say, follow the rules I gave your ancestors and have been reminding you about through my prophets."

But they just wouldn't listen. If anything, they were even more stubborn than their ancestors, which is saying something. They totally disrespected His instructions, the sacred promise He made with their ancestors, and all His warnings. They started living for nothing and basically became nothing, just like the pagan people around them. God had given them a clear warning: "Don't do it!" but they did it anyway.

They tossed out everything their God had told them. They replaced Him with two statues of bull-calves and a pole for some goddess named Asherah. They started worshipping stars and planets and were always at the sex-and-religion shrines for Baal. They even stooped so low as to sacrifice their own sons and daughters as burnt offerings! They got into all kinds of dark magic and sorcery. Basically, they sold themselves out to every evil thing they could find. And God had finally had enough.

God was so incredibly angry that He just got rid of them, kicked them out of the country for good, until only the tribe of Judah was left. (And honestly, Judah wasn't much better. They didn't follow God's commands either and fell into the same bad habits as Israel.) God rejected everyone connected to Israel, made their lives super hard, and let anyone who wanted to take advantage of them do it. And then came the final "No" as He threw them out of His sight.

This all goes back to when God ripped Israel away from David's family line, and they made Jeroboam son of Nebat their king. Jeroboam totally corrupted Israel—he turned them away from God and led them into a life full of sin. The Israelites just went along with all the sins Jeroboam introduced; they never even complained. In the end, God had to say a final "No" to Israel and turn His back on them. He had given them plenty of fair warnings through His prophets. Then He exiled Israel from their own land to Assyria. And that's where they still are today.

The king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim and moved them into the towns of Samaria to replace the exiled Israelites. They just moved in and took over like they owned the place. When these new people first got there, they treated God like just another random god; they didn't respect or worship Him. So, God sent lions that started attacking and killing them.

A message was sent back to the king of Assyria: "Hey, the people you sent to live in Samaria don't know the rules of the local god, and now he's sending lions to kill them because nobody knows what he wants."
So the king of Assyria commanded, "Send back one of the priests we exiled from there. Let him go back and live there and teach the people what the god of the land expects."
So one of the priests who had been exiled from Samaria came back and settled in Bethel. He started teaching them how to properly worship God.

But every group of people that Assyria had settled there just went ahead and made their own gods anyway. They set them up in the local shrines that the people of Samaria had left behind. It was like a custom-made god for each town.

For Babylon, it was Succoth Benoth; for Cuthah, it was Nergal; for Hamath, Ashima; for Avva, Nibhaz and Tartak; for Sepharvaim, Adrammelech and Anammelech (they would even burn their own children as sacrifices to these gods!).
for Babylon, Succoth Benoth;
for Cuthah, Nergal;
for Hamath, Ashima;
for Avva, Nibhaz and Tartak;
for Sepharvaim, Adrammelech and Anammelech (they would even burn their own children as sacrifices to these gods!).

So they were technically worshipping God, but not really. They also appointed all sorts of random people as priests to run the rituals at their local shrines. They worshipped God, but they also kept worshipping the old gods from where they came from.

And they're still doing it today, still worshipping any old god that gives them nostalgic vibes. They don't actually worship the real God—they don't take His commands seriously, the ones He revealed to the children of Jacob, who He renamed Israel. God made a covenant with them and ordered, "Don't worship other gods. Don't serve them, don't sacrifice to them. Worship ME, the God who rescued you from Egypt with my incredible power. Fear me. Worship me. Sacrifice to me. Only me! All the rules I wrote down for you—do them for your whole life. And whatever you do, don't worship other gods! Don't forget the covenant I made with you. And don't worship other gods! Worship God, and only God—He's the one who will save you from your enemies."

But they didn't listen. They just kept doing the same old things. So it turned out, while these people were pretending to worship God, they were also messing with their local idols. And they're still at it. Like father, like son.

2 Kings.title: King Hezekiah's Ultimate Trust Fail
paragraphs: So, in the third year that Hoshea was king of Israel, this guy Hezekiah, who was 25, started ruling Judah. He was king for 29 years in Jerusalem. His mom was Abijah. God actually thought he was a pretty solid king, kinda like his ancestor David. He got rid of all the weird local shrines, smashed these stone pillars people were into, and chopped down the groves where they were mixing up religion and... other stuff. He even crushed the bronze snake Moses had made way back when, because the Israelites had started sacrificing to it and even gave it a name, Nehushtan, which means 'The Old Serpent.' Lowkey, that's kinda creepy.

Hezekiah fully trusted God. Seriously, there was no other king like him, before or after. He stuck with God, never let go, and followed all the rules God gave Moses. And God had his back through everything.
He even rebelled against the king of Assyria and was like, 'Nah, I'm not serving you anymore.' He also pushed the Philistines all the way back to Gaza.

In Hezekiah's fourth year as king, the king of Assyria, Shalmaneser, attacked Samaria and laid siege to it for three years. They finally captured it in Hezekiah's sixth year. The king of Assyria then exiled the Israelites and moved them to a bunch of different places.
This all went down because they totally ignored God and didn't care about the promises they made. They just wouldn't listen or do what God's servant Moses had told them.

Fast forward to Hezekiah's fourteenth year as king. Sennacherib, the new king of Assyria, rolled up and captured all of Judah's fortified cities. Hezekiah sent a message to the Assyrian king saying, 'My bad, I messed up. Pull your army back, and I'll pay whatever you want.'

The king of Assyria demanded a crazy amount of silver and gold. Hezekiah had to give him all the silver from the Temple and the palace. He even stripped the gold from the Temple doors and gave it to the Assyrian king. Wild.
But the king of Assyria still sent his top three generals with a huge army to Jerusalem. They stopped by the aqueduct and started yelling for King Hezekiah.

Three of Hezekiah's top officials went out to meet them. The main spokesman for the Assyrians, the Rabshakeh, said, 'Tell Hezekiah that the great king of Assyria says you're living in a fantasy world. You think just talking about God is a substitute for a real army? You rebelled against my master, so who's gonna help you now? Egypt? Lol. They're a joke. And don't give me that 'we trust in God' line. Didn't you just tear down a bunch of his shrines?'

'So, for real, make a deal. I'll give you 2,000 horses if you can even find guys to ride them. You can't. So how are you gonna stop even one of my soldiers? You're still hoping for those Egyptian chariots, aren't you? Pathetic.'
'And you think I came here without God's permission? God literally told me to come and destroy this place!'
Hezekiah's officials were like, 'Bro, can you please speak in Aramaic? We understand it. Don't speak in Hebrew, everyone on the city wall can hear you.'
But the Rabshakeh was like, 'Nah, this message is for everyone. If you guys don't surrender, you'll be eating your own poop and drinking your own pee.' Super gross, right?

Then he yelled in Hebrew so everyone could hear, 'Listen to the king of Assyria! Don't let Hezekiah trick you. He can't save you. Don't listen to his whole 'God will save us' speech. Make a deal with me and you'll all get your own land and live a good life. I'll take you to a way better place than this.'

'No cap, don't listen to Hezekiah's lies. Has any god ever saved a nation from the king of Assyria? Where are the gods of all those other cities we conquered? So what makes you think your God can save Jerusalem from me?'
The people were dead silent. The king had told them not to say a word.
Then Hezekiah's officials, totally devastated, tore their clothes and went back to tell him everything the Rabshakeh had said.

2 Kings.title: God vs. the Trash-Talking King
paragraphs: When King Hezekiah heard what the messenger said, he totally freaked out and tore his clothes. He put on some really uncomfortable burlap clothes and went straight to God's Temple.
Then he sent his top palace guy, Eliakim, his secretary, Shebna, and the head priests—all wearing the same scratchy burlap—to the prophet Isaiah.
They told Isaiah, "Hezekiah says this is a dark day, a total disaster. It feels like we're about to have a baby but have zero strength to push.
Hopefully, your God heard all the trash the Assyrian king's messenger was talking, making fun of the living God. Maybe your God will shut him down. Could you please pray for the people who are left?"
So, that was the message Hezekiah's crew gave to Isaiah.
Isaiah told them, "Go tell your boss, 'God says: Don't even worry about the garbage you heard from the Assyrian king's suck-up messengers. It's all just talk.'
'Here’s my plan: I'm gonna mess with his head. He'll hear a rumor that makes him run back to his own country scared for his life. And once he's there, I'll make sure he gets taken out.'"

The Assyrian messenger bounced and found his king fighting a different city, Libnah, since he'd left Lachish. Then the Assyrian king, Sennacherib, heard that the king of Cush was coming to fight him. So he sent another message to Hezekiah, saying:

"Don't let your god, the one you trust so much, play you by saying, 'Jerusalem won't fall to the king of Assyria.' That's a straight-up lie. You know my track record—I've destroyed country after country. What makes you think you're special?

Look at all the nations my ancestors wrecked. Did their gods save them? Check out Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the people of Eden. All ruins. And what's left of the kings of Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena, or Ivvah? Just bones."
Hezekiah took the letter, read it, and then went to God's Temple. He spread the letter out right there in front of God.
And Hezekiah prayed like he'd never prayed before.

"God of Israel, who sits on a throne above the angels, you are the one and only God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made heaven and earth. Please, God, listen up. Open your eyes and see this. Look at this letter Sennacherib sent, straight-up insulting the living God!

It's true, God. The kings of Assyria have wrecked nations. They burned up their gods in huge bonfires—because they weren't real gods, just statues made of wood and stone. But now, our God, please save us from Assyria's power. Make every kingdom on earth know that you are the one and only God."
It wasn't long before Isaiah sent a message back to Hezekiah.
"God's word: I heard your prayer about King Sennacherib of Assyria. Here's my answer to him:

'The precious city of Jerusalem thinks you're a joke; they're laughing at you behind your back. Who do you think you've been insulting and bad-mouthing? Who do you think you've been flexing on? The Holy One of Israel, that's who!

You sent your little messengers to disrespect the Master. You bragged, ‘With my fleet of chariots, I’ve conquered the highest mountains, even the snowy peaks of Lebanon! I’ve chopped down its best trees. I’ve traveled everywhere, seen the coolest places. I’ve dug wells in the middle of nowhere and drunk foreign water; I’ve walked through the rivers of Egypt.’

Did it ever cross your mind that I'm the one behind all this? I planned this a long, long time ago, and now I'm making it happen. I used you like a weapon to turn proud cities into piles of rocks, leaving their people feeling weak and useless, like weeds.

I know everything you do. I see you when you sit, when you come, and when you go. And yeah, I've seen every single one of your temper tantrums against me. Because of that attitude, that disrespectful, foul temper of yours, I'm putting a hook in your nose and a bit in your mouth and dragging you right back where you came from.'"
"And this, Hezekiah, is the sign that will prove it to you:

This year, you'll eat whatever grows on its own. Next year, you'll have to scrounge for food. But in the third year, you'll plant and harvest, grow vineyards and eat grapes. The survivors of Judah will be like a tree that puts down deep roots and produces fruit.
The survivors will come from Jerusalem, from Mount Zion. God's passion will make this happen.
So, here's the bottom line from God about the king of Assyria:

'He won't get into this city. He won't even shoot a single arrow at it. He won't raise a shield against it or build a ramp to attack it. He'll go home the same way he came. He's not getting in. That's God's word! I will protect this city and save it, for my own sake and for my servant David's sake.'"
And that very night, an angel of God went to the Assyrian camp and took out 185,000 soldiers. When the people of Jerusalem woke up the next morning, they saw a whole field of dead bodies.

Sennacherib, the king of Assyria, got out of there fast. He went straight home to Nineveh and stayed there. Then one day, while he was worshiping in the temple of his god Nisroch, his own sons, Adrammelech and Sharezer, killed him. They escaped to the land of Ararat, and his son Esarhaddon became the new king.

2 Kings.title: Hezekiah's Near-Death Experience Was WILD
paragraphs: So, a little while later, Hezekiah got deathly ill. The prophet Isaiah, son of Amoz, came to him and was like, “Yo, God says to get your stuff in order, because you’re about to die. You don’t have much time left.”
Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to God.
He was like, “Please, God, remember me! Remember how I’ve lived an honest life in front of you, how my heart has been loyal and steady, and how I’ve always tried to do what makes you happy.”
And then he just broke down and cried his eyes out.

Isaiah was on his way out and wasn't even halfway across the courtyard when a message from God stopped him: “Go back and tell Hezekiah, the leader of my people, ‘This is a message from God, the God of your ancestor David: I heard your prayer and I saw your tears. I’m going to heal you. In three days, you’ll be walking into God's Temple. I’m adding fifteen years to your life, and I’m protecting you and this city from the king of Assyria. I’m defending this city for my own honor and for my servant David.’'
Then Isaiah said, “Get a plaster of figs and put it on him.”
So they made the fig plaster, put it on his infected sore, and Hezekiah started getting better.
Hezekiah asked Isaiah, “How will I know this is really from God and not just the figs? What’s the sign that God is healing me and that I’ll be walking into the Temple in three days?”
Isaiah said, “This will be your sign from God that he’s gonna do what he promised: Do you want the shadow on the sundial to jump forward ten steps or go backward ten steps? You pick.”
Hezekiah was like, “Making the shadow go forward is easy. Make it go back ten steps.”
So Isaiah prayed to God, and God made the shadow go back ten steps on Ahaz's sundial.

Not long after this, Merodach-baladan, the son of King Baladan of Babylon, heard that Hezekiah had been sick, so he sent him a get-well card and a gift. Hezekiah was super flattered and gave the messengers a full tour of his treasury—the silver, gold, spices, expensive oils, his armory, everything. He showed them all his prized possessions. There wasn't a single thing in his palace or kingdom that Hezekiah didn't show off to them.
Then Isaiah the prophet came to King Hezekiah and asked, “So, what did those guys want? Where’d they come from?”
Hezekiah said, “They came from a country far away—from Babylon.”
“And what did they see in your palace?” Isaiah asked.
“Everything,” said Hezekiah. “I gave them the grand tour. There isn’t anything in my treasury I didn’t show them.”

Then Isaiah told Hezekiah, “Listen to what God has to say about this: A day is coming when everything in your palace, all the stuff your ancestors have collected until now, will be looted and carried off to Babylon. Nothing will be left, God’s word. And even worse, some of your own sons, your own flesh and blood, will be taken away and made into eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.”
Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “The message from God you’ve given me is good.” But he was lowkey thinking to himself, “Well, at least there will be peace and security in my lifetime.”

The rest of Hezekiah’s story, all his accomplishments, including how he built the reservoir and the tunnel to bring water into the city, are all written down in the official records of the kings of Judah. Hezekiah died and was buried with his ancestors, and his son Manasseh became the next king.

2 Kings.title: Worst King Ever? Manasseh's Messed-Up Reign
paragraphs: So, Manasseh was just twelve when he got the crown, and he reigned in Jerusalem for a wild fifty-five years. His mom's name was Hephzibah. And straight up, in God's eyes, he was a terrible king. Like, seriously evil. He brought back all the gross and corrupt stuff that had been cleaned out of the country when God kicked out the pagan nations for the Israelites. He even rebuilt all the sketchy shrines for sex and religion that his own dad, Hezekiah, had torn down. He made altars and statues for the gross gods Baal and Asherah, just like King Ahab of Israel did. He was super into astrology and worshiping stars, taking his cues from the constellations. He even had the nerve to build these pagan altars right inside God's Temple, the same temple in Jerusalem that God had specifically said was for His name only. He put shrines to the stars in both courtyards of God's Temple. It gets worse—he literally sacrificed his own son by burning him. He was into black magic, fortune-telling, and even held séances to talk to spirits. God saw it as a whole career of doing evil, and He was not happy.

And for the final, most disrespectful move, he put a carved statue of the sex goddess Asherah right in God's Temple. This was a huge slap in the face to God, who had clearly told David and Solomon, 'In this Temple and in Jerusalem, which I chose from all the tribes of Israel, I will put my Name forever. I'll never make my people wander from this land I gave their ancestors again.' But there was a catch: they had to actually follow all the rules He gave them through Moses.
But did the people listen? Nope. Manasseh totally led them astray, and they ended up doing things that were even more evil than the pagan nations God had gotten rid of before.

God was completely done with it all. He sent his prophets to deliver a message: 'Because King Manasseh of Judah has done all these disgusting things, making the sins of the Amorites look like nothing and setting new records for evil, and because he used his nasty idols to turn Judah into a nation of sinners, this is what's going to happen. I, the God of Israel, am bringing a disaster on Jerusalem and Judah so bad that anyone who hears about it will be like, 'No way, I can't even believe that.'

'I'm going to give Jerusalem the same treatment Samaria got, a total repeat of what happened to Ahab. I'm gonna wipe Jerusalem clean like you'd wipe a plate, and then flip it over to dry. I'm ditching what's left of my people and handing them over to their enemies. If their enemies can get anything out of them, good for them. They've been nothing but a headache for me since the day their ancestors left Egypt. They've pushed me to my breaking point, and I'm not putting up with their evil anymore.'

The final verdict on Manasseh was that he was a straight-up murderer who killed indiscriminately. He filled Jerusalem with the blood of innocent people. And that was on top of all the sin he dragged his people into. As far as God was concerned, he turned the whole nation into sinners.

The rest of Manasseh's story, everything he did, and his sad, sinful record are all written down in The Chronicles of the Kings of Judah. Manasseh died and was buried in the palace garden, the Garden of Uzza. His son Amon became the next king.

Amon was twenty-two when he became king, and he only lasted two years in Jerusalem. His mom was Meshullemeth, the daughter of Haruz from Jotbah. In God's book, he was just as evil as his dad Manasseh. He just copied his father, worshiping the same disgusting gods. He completely bailed on the God of his ancestors and didn't live God's way at all.

Then, Amon's own servants turned on him and assassinated him right in his own palace. But then the people of the land took out the conspirators who killed King Amon and made his son, Josiah, the new king.
The rest of Amon's life is written in The Chronicles of the Kings of Judah. They buried him in his tomb in the Garden of Uzza, and his son Josiah took over as king.

2 Kings.title: King Finds Ancient Scroll & Totally Freaks Out
paragraphs: Josiah was just a kid, only eight years old, when he became king. He ruled in Jerusalem for thirty-one years. His mom was Jedidah, the daughter of Adaiah from Bozkath. He genuinely tried to live in a way that honored God, following the path of his ancestor David without messing up.

One day, in the eighteenth year of his rule, King Josiah sent his royal secretary, Shaphan, to the Temple of God. He told him, "Go find Hilkiah the high priest and have him count up all the money that people have donated to the Temple, the cash the doorkeepers have collected. Then, give that money to the project managers overseeing the Temple's renovation. They need to pay the workers—carpenters, builders, and masons. Also, give them the green light to buy lumber and stone for the repairs. Don't even worry about receipts; these guys are all trustworthy."

The high priest Hilkiah hit up Shaphan, the royal secretary, with some major news: "Yo, I just found the Book of God's Law, the one that tells us how to live. Found it right here in the Temple!" He handed the scroll to Shaphan, who started reading it.
Shaphan, the secretary, went back to the king to give him the update. "Your crew has gathered all the money from the Temple and handed it over to the foremen to pay the workers," he reported.
Then Shaphan dropped the bombshell: "By the way, Hilkiah the priest gave me a book." And he started reading it out loud to the king.

When the king heard the words from the book, God's own law, he completely lost it and ripped his clothes in distress. He immediately summoned Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Acbor son of Micaiah, Shaphan the secretary, and his personal advisor Asaiah. He ordered them, "Go pray to God for me, for the people, for all of Judah! We need to know what to do after hearing what's in this book. God must be seriously furious with us. Our ancestors clearly didn't follow any of the rules in this book, none of the instructions meant for us."

So Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam, Acbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah went straight to Huldah the prophetess. She was married to Shallum, who was in charge of the royal wardrobe, and they lived in the Second Quarter of Jerusalem. The five men went to consult her. She told them, "This is a message from the LORD, the God of Israel: Go tell the man who sent you that I am about to bring disaster on this place and its people. Every single word written in the book the king of Judah read will come true. Why? Because they've abandoned me for other gods and have made me sick with all their idol-making businesses. My anger is burning white-hot against this place, and no one can stop it.

"But, as for the king of Judah who sent you to ask for God's guidance, tell him this. God's take on the book he read is: 'Because you took the warning of doom seriously, and because you humbled yourself, tore your clothes, and cried before me, I've heard you. This is God's promise: I'll take care of you. You will die in peace and be buried quietly. You won't have to witness the disaster I'm bringing on this place.'"
The men brought her message back to the king.

2 Kings.title: King J's Total Spiritual Reset
paragraphs: The king wasted no time. He got all the leaders from Judah and Jerusalem together. Then, he headed straight for God's Temple with his whole crew—we're talking priests, prophets, and basically everyone, from the VIPs to the nobodies. He then read the entire Book of the Covenant, which they'd found in the Temple, out loud for everyone to hear. The king stood by a pillar and made a serious promise to God. He committed everyone to follow God, obey His rules with all their heart, and actually live out the stuff written in the book. The people were all in, giving a unanimous 'yes.'

Then the king told Hilkiah the high priest and his crew to do a major clean-up of the Temple. They had to toss out everything made for worshiping Baal, Asherah, and all those cosmic powers. He had it all burned outside Jerusalem in the Kidron Valley and got rid of the ashes in Bethel. He fired all the pagan priests the old kings had hired for their local shrines. He basically swept the whole country clean of the nasty stuff associated with the 24/7 worship of Baal, the sun, moon, and stars. He even took the gross Asherah pole from the Temple, burned it in the Kidron Valley, ground it to dust, and scattered the ashes in a public cemetery. He also tore down the rooms in the Temple where male prostitutes worked, which women also used for their weaving projects for Asherah. He got rid of priests from all the towns in Judah and destroyed their shrines from one end of the country to the other. He even smashed the shrine at the city gate that was for the private use of the mayor, Joshua. These priests might not have been messing with the main Altar in the Temple, but they were still part of the problem and had to go.

Josiah then wrecked the Topheth, that iron griddle in the Valley of Ben Hinnom where people were sacrificing their kids in fire. No more burning sons or daughters for the god Molech. He got rid of the horse statues honoring the sun god that Judah's kings had put up near the Temple entrance and burned the sun-chariots. Total junk.

The king went on a rampage, smashing all the altars. The ones on the roof shrine of Ahaz, the ones the kings of Judah had built, and the ones Manasseh had put all over the Temple courtyard—he pulverized them all and scattered the dust in the Kidron Valley. He also cleared out all the shrines Solomon had built for the gross Sidonian goddess Ashtoreth, the creepy Moabite god Chemosh, and the messed-up Ammonite god Milcom. He smashed the altars, chopped down the Asherah poles, and threw old bones all over the sites. Next, he went after the altar at Bethel that Jeroboam, the guy who led Israel into sin, had built. He tore it apart, burned it to ashes, and set the Asherah pole on fire.

While Josiah was looking around, he saw some tombs on a hill. He had the bones taken out and burned on the ruined altars to make them unholy. This was exactly what a man of God had predicted years ago when Jeroboam was standing by that same altar.
Then the king asked, 'Whose memorial stone is that?'
The city guys told him, 'That's the grave of the man of God who predicted all this stuff you're doing to the altar at Bethel.'
Josiah said, 'Leave his bones alone.' So they didn't touch his bones, or the bones of the prophet from Samaria who was buried with him.

But Josiah wasn't done. He went through all the towns in Samaria and destroyed the shrines the kings of Israel had built, the ones that made God so angry. He killed all the priests who worked at those shrines and burned their bodies on their own altars to make them unholy. Only after all that did he go back to Jerusalem.
The king then gave a command to all the people: 'Celebrate the Passover to your God, just like it says in this Book of the Covenant.'

This was a big deal. The Passover hadn't been celebrated like this since the time of the judges—none of the kings of Israel or Judah had done it. But in the eighteenth year of King Josiah's reign, they celebrated this Passover to God in Jerusalem.

Josiah did a total spiritual cleanse. He got rid of all the spirit-mediums, sorcerers, household gods, and idols—all the nasty stuff you could find in Judah and Jerusalem. He did all this to obey the words written in the book that Hilkiah the priest had found in the Temple.

There was no king quite like Josiah, before or after him. He turned back to God completely—heart, mind, and soul—and followed all the instructions from Moses. The world would never see another king like him.

But even with all that, God was still furious. His anger, sparked by Manasseh's evil deeds, was still burning. God said, 'I'm going to get rid of Judah just like I got rid of Israel. I'm turning my back on Jerusalem, the city I chose, and this Temple where I said my Name would live.'

The rest of Josiah's story is written in the official records of the kings of Judah. He died when Pharaoh Neco of Egypt went to team up with the king of Assyria. King Josiah tried to stop him at Megiddo, but Neco killed him. His servants took his body back to Jerusalem in a chariot and buried him in his own tomb. The people then chose Josiah's son, Jehoahaz, to be the next king.
Jehoahaz was 23 when he became king, but he only lasted for three months in Jerusalem. His mom was Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah from Libnah.
God's verdict on him? He was an evil king, just like his ancestors.

Pharaoh Neco captured Jehoahaz at Riblah and put him in chains so he couldn't rule in Jerusalem. He made Judah pay a crazy amount of silver and gold as a tribute. Then Pharaoh Neco put Eliakim, another of Josiah's sons, on the throne and changed his name to Jehoiakim. As for Jehoahaz, he was dragged off to Egypt and died there.
Meanwhile, Jehoiakim acted like a good little puppet and paid the silver and gold Pharaoh demanded. He got the money by taxing the people, forcing everyone to pay up.

Jehoiakim was 25 when he started his rule, and he was king in Jerusalem for eleven years. His mother was Zebidah from Rumah. And in God's eyes, he was another evil king, following in the footsteps of his ancestors.

2 Kings.title: Judah's Downfall: The Final Betrayal
paragraphs: So, while this dude Jehoiakim was king, the Babylonian king, Nebuchadnezzar, rolled in and took over. Jehoiakim basically became his little puppet. But after three years, he was like, 'Nah, I'm done with this,' and rebelled.

Then God sent a bunch of different crews to mess with him – Babylonians, Arameans, Moabites, and Ammonites. The whole point was to wreck Judah. God had been warning them this would happen through his prophets, and now it was going down. This wasn't random, either. It was God's judgment because he was so done with Judah after all the messed-up stuff King Manasseh did. That guy was a straight-up killer who had innocent people's blood running in the streets of Jerusalem. God was not going to let that slide.
If you want the full scoop on Jehoiakim, it's all in 'The Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.' Anyway, he died and was buried, and his son Jehoiachin took over as king.

Egypt wasn't a problem anymore. Their king wasn't invading because the Babylonian king had already snatched up all the land from the Egyptian border all the way to the Euphrates River, which used to be Egypt's turf.
Jehoiachin was 18 when he became king, but he only lasted in Jerusalem for three months. His mom was Nehushta from Jerusalem. And yeah, God thought he was a bad king too, just like his dad.

The next thing you know, King Nebuchadnezzar's crew attacked Jerusalem and had it surrounded. While they were doing that, Nebuchadnezzar himself showed up. So, King Jehoiachin of Judah, along with his mom, his officials, and all his leaders, just gave up.

In the eighth year of his reign, the king of Babylon took Jehoiachin prisoner. Nebuchadnezzar cleaned out the treasuries of God's Temple and the palace, and he jacked all the gold stuff that King Solomon had made for the Temple. This shouldn't have been a shocker, though—God had said it would happen. Then he kicked a ton of people out of Jerusalem—all the leaders, soldiers, craftsmen, and artisans. He sent like ten thousand of them into exile! The only people left were the super poor.

He dragged Jehoiachin off to Babylon. He also took the king's mom, his wives, his top officials, and all the important people. It was like seven thousand soldiers and a thousand craftsmen and artisans, all forced to move to Babylon.
Then the king of Babylon made Jehoiachin’s uncle, Mattaniah, the new puppet king and changed his name to Zedekiah.
Zedekiah was 21 when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for eleven years. His mom was Hamutal from Libnah.
As far as God was concerned, Zedekiah was just another bad king, a total copy of Jehoiakim.
All this disaster happened to Jerusalem and Judah because God was so angry. He just turned his back on them. And then, to top it all off, Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

2 Kings.title: The Absolute Worst Ending Ever
paragraphs: So, in King Zedekiah's ninth year, things got real. King Nebuchadnezzar rolled up to Jerusalem with his entire army, like, no warning. They set up camp and basically trapped everyone inside the city. For 19 months, Jerusalem was on lockdown. By year 11 of Zedekiah's reign, the hunger was insane. We're talking zero food, not even crumbs. Then, a breakout. The whole army bounced in the middle of the night through a secret opening in the wall. They snuck past the Babylonian guards and made a run for the Jordan Valley. But the Babylonians were on them and caught up to King Zedekiah in Jericho. By that point, his army had totally bailed on him and scattered. The Babylonians captured Zedekiah and dragged him to the king of Babylon. They put him on trial right then and there. And then, the unthinkable: they executed his sons right in front of him. That was the last thing he ever saw, because then they blinded him. They put him in cuffs and shipped him off to Babylon. Wild.

Fast forward to Nebuchadnezzar's 19th year as king. His top guy, Nebuzaradan, showed up in Jerusalem. And he went on a rampage. He torched God's Temple, the king's palace, and then the rest of the city. The whole place was literally up in flames. He had his Babylonian soldiers tear down the city walls. Then he rounded up everyone still in the city, even the people who had switched sides to join the Babylonians, and sent them all into exile. He only left a few poor farmers to take care of the vineyards and fields.

The Babylonians broke apart the bronze pillars, the bronze washing stands, and the giant bronze basin from God's Temple and hauled all the bronze to Babylon. They also took all the fancy bronze accessories used in the Temple services, plus the gold and silver incense burners and bowls. The king's deputy didn't leave anything behind—he took every piece of valuable metal he could find.

The amount of bronze they got from the two pillars, the basin, and all the washstands that Solomon had made for God's Temple was insane—they couldn't even weigh it all! Each pillar was 27 feet tall, with another 4.5 feet of fancy bronze designs on top.

The king's deputy also took some important people as prisoners: Seraiah the head priest, Zephaniah the priest under him, three guards, the top army officer left, five of the king's advisors, the accountant, the army's main recruiter, and sixty other important guys from the city. Nebuzaradan, the king's deputy, marched them all to the king of Babylon at Riblah. And there, in Riblah, the king of Babylon had them all killed. No mercy.
Judah was sent into exile, kicked out of their own land.

As for the regular people left in Judah, King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon put a guy named Gedaliah, son of Ahikam, in charge of them. When the army officers who were still around heard about this, they went to meet Gedaliah at Mizpah. These guys included Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Johanan son of Kareah, Seraiah son of Tanhumeth, and Jaazaniah son of the Maacathite, along with their followers.

Gedaliah promised the officers and their men, 'Don't be scared of the Babylonian officials. Just go back to your farms and families and show respect to the king of Babylon. Trust me, it's all gonna be okay.'

But then, a little while later, in the seventh month, Ishmael son of Nethaniah, who was actually from the royal family, came back with ten men and killed Gedaliah, the Jewish traitors, and the Babylonian officials who were at Mizpah. It was a total bloodbath.
After that, everyone got scared of what the Babylonians would do, so they all dipped and went to Egypt—leaders and regular people, everyone.

Thirty-seven years after King Jehoiachin of Judah was taken into exile, a new king named Evil-Merodach came to power in Babylon and let Jehoiachin out of prison. This happened on the 27th day of the twelfth month. The king was super nice to him and gave him better treatment than any of the other political prisoners in Babylon. Jehoiachin got to take off his prison clothes and ate with the king for the rest of his life. The king gave him everything he needed to live a comfortable life.

1 Chronicles.title: The Ultimate Family Tree Reveal: From Adam to the Kings
paragraphs: Adam
Mahalalel
Methuselah
Lamech
Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
Japheth's kids were Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras.
Gomer's kids were Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah.
Javan's kids were Elisha, Tarshish, Kittim, and Rodanim.
Ham's kids were Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan.
Cush's kids were Seba, Havilah, Sabta, Raamah, and Sabteca.
Raamah's kids were Sheba and Dedan.
Cush was also the father of Nimrod, who was like the first big hero on Earth.
Mizraim was the ancestor of the Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim, Casluhim, and the Caphtorim (where the Philistines came from).
Canaan was the father of Sidon (his first son) and Heth. He was also the ancestor of the Jebusites, Amorites, Girgashites, Hivites, Arkites, Sinites, Arvadites, Zemarites, and Hamathites.
Shem's crew was Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud, Aram, Uz, Hul, Gether, and Meshech.
Arphaxad had Shelah, and Shelah had Eber. Eber had two sons: one was named Peleg, which means 'Division,' because back in his day, the whole world got split up. His brother was Joktan.
Joktan's sons were Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, Ebal, Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab—that's the whole Joktan squad.
So, to recap the main family lines: Shem, Arphaxad, Shelah, Eber, Peleg, Reu, Serug, Nahor, Terah, and then Abram, who you probably know as Abraham. And Abraham had two sons, Isaac and Ishmael.

Abraham's family tree branched out from there. Ishmael's first son was Nebaioth, then Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam, Mishma, Dumah, Massa, Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah. That's the Ishmael side of the family.

Abraham also had kids with his other wife, Keturah. She had Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. Then Jokshan had Sheba and Dedan. And Midian's kids were Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. That's the Keturah branch.

Abraham had Isaac, and Isaac had two sons, Esau and Israel (who was also called Jacob). Esau's sons were Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. Eliphaz's sons were Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, Kenaz, Timna, and Amalek. And Reuel's sons were Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah.

Then there was Seir, whose sons were Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan. Lotan's sons were Hori and Homam, and Timna was Lotan's sister. Shobal's sons were Alian, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam. Zibeon's sons were Aiah and Anah. Anah's son was Dishon. Dishon's sons were Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Keran. Ezer's sons were Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan. And Dishan's sons were Uz and Aran.
Here's a list of the kings who were in charge in the land of Edom before Israel even had a king:
First up was Bela, son of Beor. His city was Dinhabah.
After Bela died, the next king was Jobab, son of Zerah from Bozrah.
After Jobab died, the next king was Husham from the land of the Temanites.
After Husham died, the next king was Hadad, son of Bedad. This was the guy who beat Midian in Moab. His city was Avith.
After Hadad died, the next king was Samlah from Masrekah.
After Samlah died, the next king was Shaul from Rehoboth-by-the-River.
After Shaul died, the next king was Baal-Hanan, son of Acbor.
After Baal-Hanan died, the next king was Hadad. His city was Pau, and his wife was Mehetabel, who was the daughter of Matred, who was the daughter of Me-Zahab.
And then, finally, Hadad died.

After all that, the chiefs of Edom were Chief Timna, Chief Alvah, Chief Jetheth, Chief Oholibamah, Chief Elah, Chief Pinon, Chief Kenaz, Chief Teman, Chief Mibzar, Chief Magdiel, and Chief Iram. Those were the main dudes in Edom.

1 Chronicles.title: The Ultimate Family Tree Reveal
paragraphs: Alright, so here's the rundown of Israel's (aka Jacob's) sons: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Dan, Joseph, Benjamin, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher.

Okay, so Judah had three sons, Er, Onan, and Shelah, with his wife Bathshua, who was from Canaan. But get this, Judah's first son, Er, was so out of line that God literally just took him out. Then, in a wild turn of events, Judah had two more sons, Perez and Zerah, with his daughter-in-law Tamar. So, five sons for Judah in total. From there, Perez had Hezron and Hamul. Zerah had five sons: Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol, and Darda. Then there was this guy Carmi, whose son Achar messed up big time by breaking a sacred rule and basically cursed all of Israel. Not a good look. Ethan's son was Azariah. And Hezron's sons were Jerahmeel, Ram, and Chelubai.

Ram's son was Amminadab, and his son was Nahshon, who was a big deal in the Judah tribe. Nahshon's line went Salmon, then Boaz, then Obed, then Jesse. Jesse’s firstborn was Eliab, then Abinadab, Shimea, Nethanel, Raddai, Ozem, and finally David, who was the seventh. They had two sisters, Zeruiah and Abigail. Zeruiah had three sons: Abishai, Joab, and Asahel. Abigail had a son named Amasa, and his dad was Jether the Ishmaelite.

Hezron's son Caleb had kids with his wife Azubah and also with Jerioth. Azubah's sons were Jesher, Shobab, and Ardon. After Azubah passed away, Caleb married Ephrath, and they had a son named Hur. Hur's son was Uri, and Uri's son was Bezalel. Later on, when Hezron was 60, he married the daughter of Makir, who was the main guy in Gilead. She had a son named Segub. Segub's son was Jair, who owned 23 cities in Gilead. But then, Geshur and Aram came and took over Jair's villages and Kenath and all their little towns—like 60 of them. All those places originally belonged to Makir's family. After Hezron died, Caleb married his dad's wife Ephrathah, and she had Ashhur, who was the founder of Tekoa.
The sons of Jerahmeel, who was Hezron's firstborn, were: Ram (the oldest), then Bunah, Oren, Ozem, and Ahijah. Jerahmeel also had another wife named Atarah, and she had a son named Onam.
Ram, Jerahmeel's firstborn, had three sons: Maaz, Jamin, and Eker.
Onam's sons were Shammai and Jada.
Shammai's sons were Nadab and Abishur. Abishur's wife was Abihail, and they had two sons, Ahban and Molid.
Nadab had two sons, Seled and Appaim. Seled died without having any kids.
Appaim's son was Ishi, Ishi's son was Sheshan, and Sheshan's son was Ahlai.
Jada, who was Shammai's brother, had two sons, Jether and Jonathan. Jether died without any kids.
Jonathan's sons were Peleth and Zaza.
So yeah, that's the whole family tree for Jerahmeel's descendants.

Sheshan didn't have any sons, just daughters. But he had an Egyptian servant named Jarha. So Sheshan had his daughter marry Jarha, and they had a son named Attai. The family line from there goes: Attai, then Nathan, then Zabad, then Ephlal, then Obed, then Jehu, then Azariah, then Helez, then Eleasah, then Sismai, then Shallum, then Jekamiah, and finally Elishama.
Jerahmeel's brother Caleb had a son, his firstborn, named Mesha. Mesha's son was Ziph, and Ziph's son was Mareshah, who founded Hebron.
Hebron's sons were: Korah, Tappuah, Rekem, and Shema. Shema's son was Raham, who founded Jorkeam. Rekem's son was Shammai.
Shammai's son was Maon, and Maon founded Beth Zur.
Caleb's concubine Ephah had three sons: Haran, Moza, and Gazez. Haran also had a son named Gazez.
Jahdai's sons were: Regem, Jotham, Geshan, Pelet, Ephah, and Shaaph.

Caleb had another concubine, Maacah, who had Sheber and Tirhanah. She also had Shaaph, who founded Madmannah, and Sheva, who founded Macbenah and Gibea. Caleb's daughter was Acsah. So that's the Caleb branch of the family tree.
The sons of Hur, who was Ephrathah's firstborn, were: Shobal (who founded Kiriath Jearim), Salma (who founded Bethlehem), and Hareph (who founded Beth Gader).

The family of Shobal, the founder of Kiriath Jearim, included Haroeh, half the people of Manahath, and the families of Kiriath Jearim—the Ithrites, the Puthites, the Shumathites, and the Mishraites. The Zorathites and Eshtaolites also came from this line.

The sons of Salma were: Bethlehem, the Netophathites, Atroth Beth Joab, half of the Manahathites, the Zorites, and the families of Sopherim who lived at Jabez—the Tirathites, the Shimeathites, and the Sucathites. These guys were the Kenites who came from Hammath, the founder of the house of Recab.

1 Chronicles.title: King David's Family Tree: The Ultimate Royal Lineup
paragraphs: So, here's the rundown on King David's sons, born while he was ruling from Hebron.
First up was Amnon, whose mom was Ahinoam from Jezreel.
Next was Daniel, from Abigail of Carmel.
Third was Absalom, son of Maacah, who was the daughter of King Talmai of Geshur.
Fourth in line was Adonijah, son of Haggith.
Fifth was Shephatiah, son of Abital.
And the sixth was Ithream, from his wife Eglah.
These were the six sons he had in Hebron, where he was king for seven and a half years.

Then he moved to Jerusalem and was king there for another 33 years. In Jerusalem, he had more sons: first Shammua, then Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon. The mother of these four was Bathsheba, the daughter of Ammiel. But wait, there's more! He had another nine sons: Ibhar, Elishua, Eliphelet, Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia, Elishama, Eliada, and another Eliphelet. These were all David's sons, and they also had a sister named Tamar. Plus, he had other sons with his concubines.

The family tree keeps going. Solomon's son was Rehoboam, whose son was Abijah, who had Asa, who had Jehoshaphat, who had Jehoram, who had Ahaziah, who had Joash, who had Amaziah, who had Azariah, who had Jotham, who had Ahaz, who had Hezekiah, who had Manasseh, who had Amon, and who had Josiah.
Josiah had a few sons himself. His first was Johanan, then Jehoiakim, then Zedekiah, and the youngest was Shallum.
Jehoiakim’s sons were Jeconiah (also called Jehoiachin) and Zedekiah.
Then Jeconiah had sons while he was a prisoner in Babylon: Shealtiel, Malkiram, Pedaiah, Shenazzar, Jekamiah, Hoshama, and Nedabiah.
Pedaiah had two sons, Zerubbabel and Shimei. Zerubbabel had Meshullam and Hananiah, and their sister was Shelomith. He also had five more sons: Hashubah, Ohel, Berekiah, Hasadiah, and Jushab-Hesed.
Hananiah's sons were Pelatiah and Jeshaiah. Then there were the sons of Rephaiah, the sons of Arnan, the sons of Obadiah, and the sons of Shecaniah.
Shecaniah had a son named Shemaiah, who had six sons: Hattush, Igal, Bariah, Neariah, and Shaphat.
Neariah had three sons: Elioenai, Hizkiah, and Azrikam.
And Elioenai had seven sons: Hodaviah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, Delaiah, and Anani.

1 Chronicles.title: This One Prayer Changed His ENTIRE Life
paragraphs: Alright, so here's the rundown on Judah's crew: Perez, Hezron, Carmi, Hur, and Shobal. Shobal's son was Reaiah, and Reaiah's sons were Jahath, Ahumai, and Lahad. These guys started the Zorathite families.

Then there were the sons of Etam: Jezreel, Ishma, and Idbash, and their sister was named Hazzelelponi. Penuel was the father of Gedor, and Ezer was the father of Hushah. These were all descendants of Hur, who was the first son of Ephrathah, the guy who basically founded Bethlehem.

Ashhur, the founder of Tekoa, had two wives, Helah and Naarah. Naarah had Ahuzzam, Hepher, Temeni, and Haahashtari—those were her kids. Helah's sons were Zereth, Zohar, Ethnan, and Koz. Koz was the ancestor of Anub, Hazzobebah, and the families of Aharhel, son of Harum.

Now, check this out: there was this guy Jabez. He was lowkey a legend, way more honorable than his brothers. His mom named him Jabez, which means 'pain,' because she went through a lot when she had him. But Jabez prayed to the God of Israel, and was like, 'Yo, for real, bless me! Give me a ton of land, and please, protect me so nothing bad can happen to me.' And God actually gave him exactly what he asked for. Wild.

Kelub, who was Shuhah's brother, had a son named Mehir. Mehir's son was Eshton, and Eshton's sons were Beth Rapha, Paseah, and Tehinnah, who founded the 'City of Smiths.' These guys were known as the men of Recah.
The sons of Kenaz were Othniel and Seraiah.
Othniel's sons were Hathath and Meonothai.
Meonothai's son was Ophrah, and Seraiah's son was Joab, who founded the 'Colony of Artisans.'
The sons of Caleb, Jephunneh's son, were Iru, Elah, and Naam.
Elah's son was Kenaz.
The sons of Jehallelel were Ziph, Ziphah, Tiria, and Asarel.

The sons of Ezrah were Jether, Mered, Epher, and Jalon. One of Mered's wives was Bithiah, who was Pharaoh's daughter. She had Miriam, Shammai, and Ishbah, the founder of Eshtemoa. His other wife, who was from Judah, had Jered, the founder of Gedor; Heber, the founder of Soco; and Jekuthiel, the founder of Zanoah.
The sons of Hodiah's wife, who was Naham's sister, were the father of Keilah the Garmite and Eshtemoa the Maacathite.
The sons of Shimon were Amnon, Rinnah, Ben-Hanan, and Tilon.
The sons of Ishi were Zoheth and Ben-Zoheth.

The sons of Shelah, who was Judah's son, were Er (the founder of Lecah), Laadah (the founder of Mareshah), the family of linen workers at Beth Ashbea, Jokim, the men of Cozeba, and Joash and Saraph, who ruled in Moab and Jashubi Lehem. This is all from super old records, btw. They were the potters who lived at Netaim and Gederah, and they worked for the king.
The Simeon family tree went like this: Nemuel, Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, and Shaul. Shaul's son was Shallum, Shallum's son was Mibsam, and Mibsam's son was Mishma.
Mishma's son was Hammuel, and Hammuel's son was Zaccur, and Zaccur's son was Shimei.

Shimei had sixteen sons and six daughters, but his brothers didn't have nearly as many kids, so their family never got as big as Judah's. They lived in a bunch of towns: Beersheba, Moladah, Hazar Shual, Bilhah, Ezem, Tolad, Bethuel, Hormah, Ziklag, Beth Marcaboth, Hazar Susim, Beth Biri, and Shaaraim. They lived there until David became king. They also had five other towns nearby—Etam, Ain, Rimmon, Token, and Ashan—and all the villages around them, all the way to Baalath. That was their territory, and they kept really good family records.

Then there's this list of leaders: Meshobab, Jamlech, Joshah son of Amaziah, Joel, Jehu son of Joshibiah (who was the son of Seraiah, son of Asiel), Elioenai, Jaakobah, Jeshohaiah, Asaiah, Adiel, Jesimiel, Benaiah, and Ziza son of Shiphi (who was the son of Allon, son of Jedaiah, son of Shimri, son of Shemaiah). All these guys were leaders in their families. They were super successful and their families grew so much that they had to go all the way to Gedor to find enough pasture for their flocks. And they found it—it was amazing pasture, super spacious, peaceful, and quiet.

Some Hamites used to live there, but when Hezekiah was king of Judah, these guys came and attacked them, wrecking their tents and houses. No cap, there was nothing left of them. Then they just moved in and took over because the land was so good for their flocks. And get this: 500 of these Simeonites, led by Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah, and Uzziel (the sons of Ishi), went and invaded the hill country of Seir. They took out all the Amalekites who had escaped and were still hanging around. And they're still living there today.

1 Chronicles.title: Israel's OG Tribes: Family Drama & Epic Battles
paragraphs: So, here's the tea on Reuben's family, Israel's oldest son. Even though Reuben was the firstborn, he totally blew it by hooking up with his own dad's side-chick. Super messed up, right? So, his firstborn rights got handed over to Joseph's sons. He basically got demoted from being the #1 kid in the family tree. And get this, even though Judah's family line became the most powerful and King David came from them, the official 'firstborn' title still went to Joseph's kids.
The sons of Reuben, Israel's firstborn, were Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.

The descendants of Joel went like this: Shemaiah, then his son Gog, his son Shimei, his son Micah, his son Reaiah, his son Baal, and his son Beerah. This guy Beerah was the leader of the Reubenites, but he got captured and taken away by Tiglath-Pileser, the king of Assyria.

Beerah's relatives are all listed in the family records by their clans: first Jeiel, then Zechariah, and then Bela son of Azaz, who was the son of Shema, who was the son of Joel. Joel's crew lived in the area from Aroer all the way to Nebo and Baal Meon. Their family owned land right up to the edge of the desert that stretches to the Euphrates River because their herds of animals got so huge they couldn't all fit in Gilead. During King Saul's time, they went to war with the Hagrites and won, taking over their camps and living there on the eastern edge of Gilead.
The Gad tribe were their neighbors in Bashan, all the way to Salecah. Joel was their top guy, Shapham was second-in-command, and then there was Janai, who was the judge in Bashan.

Their relatives, listed by families, were Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jacan, Zia, and Eber—seven of them. These were the sons of Abihail, who was the son of Huri, son of Jaroah, son of Gilead, son of Michael, son of Jeshishai, son of Jahdo, son of Buz. Ahi, son of Abdiel, who was the son of Guni, was the head of their family.
The Gad family lived in Gilead and Bashan, including the nearby towns, and their land went all the way to the pastures of Sharon.
They were all officially registered in the family tree when Jotham was king of Judah and Jeroboam was king of Israel.

The families of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh had 44,760 guys ready for war—they were all fit and knew how to use a shield, sword, and bow. They went up against the Hagrites, Jetur, Naphish, and Nodab. God had their backs while they were fighting. He basically handed the Hagrites and all their allies over to them because they cried out to him for help during the battle. God came through for them because they trusted him. They took a ton of their stuff: 50,000 camels, 250,000 sheep, and 2,000 donkeys. They also captured 100,000 people. A lot of people died, because it was God's battle. They lived in that land until they were exiled.

The half-tribe of Manasseh had a huge population. They lived in the land from Bashan to Baal Hermon, which is also Mount Hermon. The leaders of their families were Epher, Ishi, Eliel, Azriel, Jeremiah, Hodaviah, and Jahdiel—they were all brave warriors, super famous, and leaders of their families. But they weren't loyal to the God of their ancestors. They started worshipping the fake gods of the people who lived in the land before them, the ones God had gotten rid of. So the God of Israel made Pul, the king of Assyria (who was also Tiglath-Pileser), come and take the families of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh into exile. He deported them to Halah, Habor, Hara, and the Gozan river. And they've been there ever since.

1 Chronicles.title: The Levites: God's OG Worship Crew
paragraphs: Alright, so Levi's sons were Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Kohath's crew included Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. Amram's kids? The famous trio: Aaron, Moses, and Miriam. Aaron's sons were Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. Then it's a whole family tree situation: Eleazar was Phinehas's dad, Phinehas was Abishua's dad, Abishua was Bukki's dad, Bukki was Uzzi's dad, Uzzi was Zerahiah's dad, Zerahiah was Meraioth's dad, Meraioth was Amariah's dad, Amariah was Ahitub's dad, Ahitub was Zadok's dad, Zadok was Ahimaaz's dad, Ahimaaz was Azariah's dad, Azariah was Johanan's dad, and Johanan had Azariah—the one who was the priest in the temple Solomon built in Jerusalem, which was a pretty big deal. After him, the line went Azariah, then Amariah, Ahitub, Zadok, Shallum, Hilkiah, Azariah, Seraiah, and finally Jehozadak.
So, Jehozadak was the one who got hauled off into exile when God used Nebuchadnezzar to take Judah and Jerusalem away.

Okay, let's break down the Levi fam again. Levi's sons: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Gershon's sons were Libni and Shimei. Kohath's sons were Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. Merari's sons were Mahli and Mushi. These were the main Levitical clans, family by family. For Gershon's line, you had his son Libni, then his son Jehath, then Zimmah, Joah, Iddo, Zerah, and Jeatherai. For Kohath's line, it was his son Amminadab, then Korah, Assir, Elkanah, Ebiasaph, Assir again, Tahath, Uriel, Uzziah, and Shaul. Elkanah's sons were Amasai and Ahimoth. Then that line went Elkanah, Zophai, Nahath, Eliab, Jeroham, and another Elkanah. The prophet Samuel's sons were Joel, the oldest, and Abijah, the second. Merari's line went Mahli, his son Libni, his son Shimei, his son Uzzah, his son Shimea, his son Haggiah, and his son Asaiah.

These were the guys King David put in charge of the music ministry at the house of God after they brought the Ark of the Covenant there. They were basically the worship leaders at the place of worship, the Tent of Meeting, until Solomon built the actual Temple in Jerusalem. They took their jobs seriously and followed all the instructions they were given.

Here's the lineup of the main worship leaders and their sons who helped out. From the Kohathite family, you had Heman, the head choirmaster. His family tree is also crazy long, going all the way back to Levi, who was a son of Israel himself: he was the son of Joel, who was the son of Samuel, son of Elkanah, son of Jeroham, son of Eliel, son of Toah, son of Zuph, son of Elkanah, son of Mahath, son of Amasai, son of Elkanah, son of Joel, son of Azariah, son of Zephaniah, son of Tahath, son of Assir, son of Ebiasaph, son of Korah, son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, son of Israel.

Heman's right-hand man was Asaph. His family tree is also listed, tracing back to Gershon, another one of Levi's sons. Asaph was the son of Berekiah, son of Shimea, son of Michael, son of Baaseiah, son of Malkijah, son of Ethni, son of Zerah, son of Adaiah, son of Ethan, son of Zimmah, son of Shimei, son of Jahath, son of Gershon, son of Levi.

And from the Merari family, the guys who stood on the left side, was Ethan. He was the son of Kishi, son of Abdi, son of Malluch, son of Hashabiah, son of Amaziah, son of Hilkiah, son of Amzi, son of Bani, son of Shemer, son of Mahli, son of Mushi, son of Merari, son of Levi.
The rest of the Levites were given all the other jobs that needed to be done in the house of God.

Aaron and his sons were in charge of the sacrifices on the Altar of Burnt Offering and the Altar of Incense. They handled everything related to the Most Holy Place. They made things right for Israel, just like Moses, God's servant, had commanded.

And here are Aaron's descendants: his son Eleazar, his son Phinehas, his son Abishua, his son Bukki, his son Uzzi, his son Zerahiah, his son Meraioth, his son Amariah, his son Ahitub, his son Zadok, and his son Ahimaaz.

These are the places where the priestly families were given to live. The first pick went to the sons of Aaron from the Kohathite family. They got Hebron in Judah and the fields around it. But the fields and villages farther out went to Caleb, son of Jephunneh. Aaron's family also got the special 'cities of refuge' with their fields: Hebron, Libnah, Jattir, Eshtemoa, Hilen, Debir, Ashan, and Beth Shemesh. From the tribe of Benjamin, they got Geba, Alemeth, and Anathoth, with their fields. All in all, the Kohathite families got thirteen cities. The rest of the Kohathites got ten more cities from the half-tribe of Manasseh. The Gershon families got thirteen cities from the tribes of Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Manasseh in Bashan. The Merari families were given twelve cities from the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and Zebulun. So the Israelites gave the Levites these cities and their fields. They also gave out cities from the tribes of Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin by drawing lots. Some of the Kohath families got their cities from the tribe of Ephraim, including the city of refuge Shechem in the hill country, plus Gezer, Jokmeam, Beth Horon, Aijalon, and Gath Rimmon, all with their fields. The rest of the Kohathites got Aner and Bileam with their fields from the half-tribe of Manasseh.
