But Amaziah was feeling himself. He led his army into the Valley of Salt and took out ten thousand men from Seir. They captured another ten thousand, took them to the top of a cliff, and just pushed them off. They all died, smashed on the rocks below. It was brutal.

Meanwhile, the troops Amaziah had fired, still salty about missing out on the loot, went on a rampage through the towns of Judah, from Samaria all the way to Beth Horon. They killed three thousand people and took a bunch of stuff.

When Amaziah came back from wrecking the Edomites, he brought back the gods of the men of Seir and set them up as his own gods, worshiping them and burning incense. This made God furious. A prophet came with a message from God, basically a divine roast: 'What are you doing? Why would you pray to these lame gods who couldn't even save their own people from you? These gods are weaker than you are, Amaziah!'
Amaziah cut him off, saying, 'Did I ask for your opinion? Shut up or I'll have you thrown out!'
The prophet stopped talking, but he got in one last word: 'I've got it on good authority: God has decided to throw you out because of what you've done, and because you wouldn't listen to me.'
One day, Amaziah sent a message to Jehoash, the king of Israel, trying to start a fight: 'Come at me, bro. Let's settle this face-to-face!'

Jehoash, the king of Israel, replied to Amaziah with a story: 'A little thistle in Lebanon sent a message to a giant cedar tree, saying, "Let my son marry your daughter." But then a wild animal came by and just stepped on the thistle, crushing it. Just because you beat Edom, you think you're a big shot now. Go ahead and be proud, but stay home. Why are you pushing your luck? You're just asking to get wrecked, and you'll take Judah down with you.'

Amaziah wouldn't listen. It was like God had already planned for Jehoash to beat him since he'd started worshiping the gods of Edom. So Jehoash, king of Israel, came down and they faced off at Beth Shemesh in Judah. Judah got completely destroyed by Israel—all the soldiers just ran home defeated.

Jehoash of Israel captured Amaziah of Judah at Beth Shemesh. But he didn't stop there. He went on to Jerusalem and tore down about 600 feet of the city wall, from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate. He looted all the gold, silver, and anything valuable he could find in the palace and the Temple of God. He even took hostages, just to be extra. Then he went back to Samaria.

Amaziah, son of Joash, king of Judah, lived for another fifteen years after Jehoash, king of Israel, died. The rest of the story of Amaziah, from beginning to end, is written down in the official records of the kings of Judah and Israel.

In his last years, after he turned his back on God, some people in Jerusalem plotted against him, and he had to run to Lachish. But they hunted him down in Lachish and killed him there. They brought his body back on a horse and buried him with his ancestors in Jerusalem, the City of David.

2 Chronicles.title: The King Who Got Too Big for His Britches
paragraphs: So, the people of Judah picked Uzziah, who was just 16, to be the new king after his dad, Amaziah. First thing he did after his dad's funeral was to get Elath back for Judah and fix it up.

Uzziah was 16 when he started his reign, and he was king in Jerusalem for a wild 52 years. His mom was Jecoliah from Jerusalem. He was actually a pretty good dude in God's eyes, following the example of his dad Amaziah. He was lowkey serious about seeking God. He had a great mentor, the prophet Zechariah, who taught him how to live with respect for God. For as long as Zechariah was alive, Uzziah lived a godly life, and God made him super successful.

He went out and fought the Philistines, breaking through their fortress cities of Gath, Jabneh, and Ashdod. He also built up settlements around Ashdod and other Philistine areas. God had his back in his wars with the Philistines, the Arabs in Gur Baal, and the Meunites. Even the Ammonites had to pay him tribute money. Uzziah got famous, like, his rep went all the way to Egypt. He got seriously powerful.

Uzziah built up defense towers in Jerusalem at the Corner Gate, the Valley Gate, and at the corner of the wall. He also built towers and dug wells out in the countryside. He had tons of cattle in the foothills and on the plains, and farmers and vineyard workers in the hills and fields—he just loved agriculture.

On the military side of things, Uzziah had a legit army, all prepped and ready to go. They were organized into companies led by Jeiel the secretary, Maaseiah the field commander, and Hananiah from the general staff. The list of family leaders in charge of the soldiers was 2,600 strong. Under them were 307,000 backup troops, with 500 of them on high alert 24/7—a seriously strong royal defense against any enemy. Uzziah made sure they were all geared up with shields, spears, helmets, armor, bows, and slingshots. He also installed some cutting-edge military tech on the towers and corners of Jerusalem for shooting arrows and launching big rocks. He got super famous for all this—a legendary king. Everything was going his way.

But then, all that strength and success went straight to his head. He got arrogant and proud, and it led to his downfall. One day, he disrespected God by strolling into God's Temple like he owned the place and tried to burn incense on the Incense Altar himself.

The priest Azariah, with 80 other brave priests of God, tried to stop him. They confronted Uzziah, saying, “You can't do this, Uzziah! Only the priests from Aaron's line, who were set apart for this job, are allowed to burn incense. Get out of God's Temple; you're being unfaithful and this is a total disgrace!”

But Uzziah, who already had the censer in his hand, was in the middle of doing it and just got mad at the priests. He totally lost his temper, and they started arguing. And then, right in the middle of the fight, a skin disease broke out on his forehead. As soon as the chief priest Azariah and the others saw it, they rushed him out of there ASAP. He hurried out himself—he knew, right then and there, that God had struck him with the disease. Uzziah had that skin disease for the rest of his life and had to live in a separate house, in quarantine. He was banned from ever entering God's Temple again. His son Jotham took over running the royal palace and the government.

The rest of Uzziah's story, from beginning to end, was written down by the prophet Isaiah, son of Amoz. When Uzziah died, they buried him with his ancestors in a field next to the royal cemetery. Because of his skin disease, he wasn't allowed to be buried in the actual royal tombs. His son Jotham became the next king.

2 Chronicles.title: Jotham: The King Who (Mostly) Followed God
paragraphs: Jotham was 25 when he became king, and he ruled for 16 years in Jerusalem. His mom was Jerusha, Zadok's daughter. He was a good king in God's eyes, and he followed the example of his dad, Uzziah. But unlike his dad, he didn't mess around and disrespect God's Temple. The people, though, they just kept on being corrupt.

Jotham built the Upper Gate of God's Temple, made the Wall of Ophel way bigger, and built cities in the hills of Judah, with forts and towers in the forests. He even went to war with the Ammonite king and won. That year, the Ammonites had to give him over three tons of silver and a crazy amount of wheat and barley, like 65,000 bushels of each. They had to do this for the next two years, too. Jotham was so strong because he was determined to obey God, no matter what.

The rest of Jotham's story, all his wars and everything he did, it's all written down in the official records of the kings of Israel and Judah. He was 25 when he started his reign, and he was king for 16 years in Jerusalem. When Jotham died, they buried him in the City of David, and his son Ahaz took over as the next king.

2 Chronicles.title: The King Who Did EVERYTHING Wrong
paragraphs: So, this dude Ahaz was 20 when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for sixteen years. But get this, he totally didn't live right in God's eyes; he was nothing like his ancestor David. Instead, he copied the kings of Israel up north, even making metal statues to worship fake gods called Baals. He got into burning incense in this sketchy place called the Valley of Ben Hinnom and—this is wild—he even did this horrific practice of sacrificing his own sons by fire. It was a super messed-up thing he learned from the pagans God had kicked out of the land earlier. He was also all about the local shrines for sex and religion that were popping up everywhere.

God was so over it that He let the king of Aram totally wreck him. The Arameans beat him badly and dragged a bunch of prisoners off to Damascus. God also let the king of Israel have a go at him, which ended in a massive slaughter. A guy named Pekah, son of Remaliah, killed 120,000 top-tier soldiers in a single day, all because they had bailed on God, the God of their ancestors. On top of that, Zicri, a hero from Ephraim, killed the king's son Maaseiah, the palace manager Azrikam, and Elkanah, who was second-in-command to the king. And it didn't stop there—the Israelites captured 200,000 men, women, and children, plus a crazy amount of loot that they hauled back to Samaria.

There was a prophet of God named Oded in the area. He met the army as it was coming into Samaria and said, "Yo, stop right there and listen up! The God of your ancestors was mad at Judah and used you to punish them. But you guys took it way too far with your own crazy anger and now you're trying to make your own brothers and sisters from Judah and Jerusalem your slaves. Don't you see what a huge sin that is against your God? Be smart about this. Do exactly what I say—send these captives back, every single one. If you don't, you're about to find out what God's anger *really* looks like."

Some of the leaders from Ephraim—Azariah son of Jehohanan, Berekiah son of Meshillemoth, Jehizkiah son of Shallum, and Amasa son of Hadlai—stood up to the army when they got back. They said, "Don't you dare bring those captives here! We've already sinned against God, and now you're about to make our sin and guilt even worse. We're already in deep trouble, enough to trigger a huge explosion of God's anger."

So the soldiers actually listened and handed over the captives and all the stolen stuff to the leaders and the people. A few guys were chosen to take care of the prisoners. They gave clothes from the loot to those who were naked, put shoes on their feet, gave them all a good meal, and gave first aid to the injured. They put the weak ones on donkeys and escorted them all the way to Jericho, the City of Palms, bringing them back to their families. Then they went back to Samaria.

Around that time, King Ahaz hit up the king of Assyria, asking for help. The Edomites had come back and beaten Judah badly, taking a lot of captives. To make things worse, the Philistines raided the towns in the western foothills and the southern desert. They captured Beth Shemesh, Aijalon, and Gederoth, plus Soco, Timnah, and Gimzo and their villages, and just moved right in. The arrogant King Ahaz, acting like he didn't need God, had basically started a plague of wickedness. Judah was on its knees because of God, and now they were just begging for help. But the king of Assyria, Tiglath-Pileser, was no help. He came and just made things worse for Ahaz, attacking and bullying him. Desperate, Ahaz looted God's Temple, the royal palace, and every other place he could find, scraped everything together, and gave it to the king of Assyria. And he got absolutely nothing in return. No help at all.

But King Ahaz still didn't learn his lesson. At the very moment everyone was turning on him, he kept turning against God! He started offering sacrifices to the gods of Damascus. He had just been defeated by Damascus, so he thought, "Hey, if I worship the gods that helped Damascus, maybe they'll help me too." But that just made things go from bad to worse. First Ahaz was ruined, and then the whole country. He stripped God's Temple of everything valuable, boarded up the doors, and then went and set up his own pagan shrines all over Jerusalem. And not just in Jerusalem, but all over Judah—he set up local shrines to worship any and every god you could think of. And man, was God angry!

The rest of Ahaz's messed-up life, everything he did from start to finish, is written down in the official records of the kings of Judah and Israel. When Ahaz died, they buried him in Jerusalem, but he wasn't even given the honor of being buried in the royal cemetery. His son Hezekiah became the next king.

2 Chronicles.title: Hezekiah's Epic Temple Reset
paragraphs: Hezekiah was 25 when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for 29 years. His mom was Abijah, Zechariah's daughter. And God was like, 'Yeah, this guy's legit.' He followed in the footsteps of his ancestor David.

First year, first month on the job, Hezekiah fixed up the doors of God's Temple and threw them open for everyone. He got all the priests and Levites together in the east courtyard and was like, “Listen up, Levites! Get yourselves right with God, and let's give this Temple a major deep clean. Our ancestors messed up big time and basically ghosted God. They turned their backs on this place where we connect with Him and just bounced. They boarded up the doors, shut off the lights, and stopped all the worship for the God of Israel in His own holy Temple. Because of that, God got super angry and made our people a total train wreck for everyone to see, like a history lesson on what not to do. That's why our ancestors died in battle, and why our wives, sons, and daughters got captured and became slaves.

“I've decided we're making a fresh start with the God of Israel. We're gonna turn things around so He's not mad at us anymore. Guys, don't slack on this! God picked you to stand before Him, to serve, and to lead worship. This is your main gig, so do it and do it right.”

The Levites snapped to attention: a bunch of guys from the Kohathites, Merarites, Gershonites, and the families of Elizaphan, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun. They all got themselves and their relatives ready, consecrated themselves, and started cleaning the Temple just like the king—and God—told them to. The priests started from the inside and worked their way out. They cleared out all the nasty, defiling junk—pagan stuff that had no business being there—and the Levites hauled it all down to the Kidron Valley. They started the cleaning on the first day of the first month. By day eight, they'd made it to the porch. It took them eight whole days to clean and consecrate the Temple itself, and then another eight days to finish the entire complex.

Then they went to King Hezekiah and reported, “We’ve cleaned the entire Temple of God, top to bottom. That includes the Altar of Whole-Burnt-Offering and the Table of the Bread of the Presence, with all their gear. We also cleaned up and reconsecrated all the stuff King Ahaz tossed out when he was going wild. Check it out; we fixed it all up. It's all set up in front of God's Altar.”

King Hezekiah got right on it. He gathered all the city leaders and they all marched over to the Temple of God. They brought seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven male goats as an offering to make things right for the royal family, the Sanctuary, and all of Judah. He told the priests from Aaron's line to sacrifice them on God's Altar. So the priests butchered the bulls, sprinkled the blood on the Altar, and then did the same with the rams and the lambs. Finally, they brought the goats forward; the king and the whole crowd laid their hands on them. The priests then butchered them and used their blood for an Absolution-Offering at the Altar to atone for the sins of all of Israel. The king had specifically ordered this big offering for everyone.

The king had the Levites get in their positions in the Temple with their instruments—cymbals, harps, and zithers. This was all based on the original setup from David, Gad the king's seer, and Nathan the prophet; it was a command from God through his prophets. The Levites were the 'Orchestra of David,' and the priests had the trumpets.

Then Hezekiah gave the signal to start. The Whole-Burnt-Offering was placed on the Altar, and at that exact moment, the choir started singing, with the trumpets and the Davidic orchestra backing them up. The whole congregation was worshiping. The singers sang, the trumpeters played, and it all went on until the sacrifice was finished. When it was all over, the king and everyone else there bowed down and worshiped. Then King Hezekiah and the leaders told the Levites to wrap it up with some praise songs to God, using lyrics from David and Asaph the seer. They sang their praises with so much joy and reverence, kneeling as they worshiped.
Hezekiah then said, “Okay, the dedication is done—you're officially consecrated to God. Now you're good to go. Come on up and bring your sacrifices and Thank-Offerings to the Temple of God.”

And man, did they come. The whole congregation brought sacrifices and Thank-Offerings. Some people were feeling so generous they even brought Whole-Burnt-Offerings. We're talking a crazy amount of generosity: seventy bulls, a hundred rams, and two hundred lambs—all for burnt offerings to God! The total number of animals consecrated for sacrifice that day was 600 bulls and 3,000 sheep. They actually ran out of qualified priests to handle all the burnt offerings, so their Levite brothers had to step in and help while more priests got consecrated. Turns out, the Levites had been more on top of getting themselves properly consecrated than the priests were. On top of all the burnt offerings, there were also the best cuts of meat for the Peace-Offerings and tons of drink offerings that went with them. Worship at the Temple of God was back on solid ground!
Hezekiah and the whole congregation were celebrating like crazy. God had set up a solid foundation for the people's lives—and it all happened so fast!

2 Chronicles.title: Hezekiah's Epic Passover Party!
paragraphs: So, King Hezekiah decided to throw a massive Passover party for God, and he invited literally everyone from Israel and Judah. He even sent out personal invites to Ephraim and Manasseh to come to God's Temple in Jerusalem. They had to move the party to the second month because not enough priests were ready and people needed more time to get to Jerusalem. Everyone was cool with the new date, and they sent out invites all over the country, from Beersheba in the south to Dan in the north. The message was basically, 'Come celebrate Passover for the God of Israel in Jerusalem.' This was a huge deal because no one alive had ever celebrated it the right way.

The king gave the command, and messengers took the invites from him and his leaders all over Israel and Judah. The invitation said: 'Yo, Israelites! Come back to God—the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel. That way, He can come back to you guys who survived the attacks from the kings of Assyria. Don't make the same mistakes your ancestors did when they ditched God, the God of their ancestors. He wrecked them for it, and you can see the proof all around you. Don't be stubborn like they were. Take God's hand. Come to His holy Temple, which is set apart for Him forever. Serve your God. Then He won't be so angry with you anymore. If you come back to God, your family and kids who were taken captive will be shown mercy and allowed to come home. Your God is super gracious and kind and won't ghost you—if you come back, He'll welcome you with open arms.'

So the messengers went from city to city through Ephraim and Manasseh, all the way up to Zebulun. But a lot of people just laughed at them and thought it was a joke. But not everyone! Some people from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun weren't too proud to come to Jerusalem. Things were way better in Judah, though. God worked in a powerful way to get everyone on the same page, and they all followed the king's and officials' orders, which were backed up by God's word.

A huge crowd showed up in Jerusalem in the second month to celebrate the Passover, which is also called the Feast of Unleavened Bread. The first thing they did was get rid of all the pagan altars in Jerusalem—they dragged them out and dumped them in the Kidron Valley. Then, on the fourteenth day of the second month, they sacrificed the Passover lambs. The priests and Levites hadn't been ready, but now they were embarrassed about being lazy, so they consecrated themselves and brought burnt offerings to God's Temple. Once they were ready, they took their places like the Law of Moses said. The priests sprinkled the blood that the Levites gave them. Since a lot of people in the crowd hadn't consecrated themselves and weren't qualified, the Levites had to handle the Passover lamb sacrifices to make sure they were properly dedicated to God.

There were a ton of people, especially from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun, who ate the Passover meal even though they hadn't properly prepared. Hezekiah prayed for them, saying, 'May God, who is all good, forgive everyone who is sincerely trying to follow Him, the God of our ancestors. Especially these people who didn't follow the exact rules for entering the Temple.'
God heard Hezekiah's prayer and healed the people.

All the Israelites in Jerusalem celebrated the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days with crazy enthusiasm. The Levites and priests praised God every single day, making a ton of noise with percussion and brass instruments. Hezekiah gave a shout-out to the Levites for doing such an awesome job leading the worship.
After the seven-day festival of worship, offerings, and praising God was over, they decided to keep the party going for another seven days! So they just kept celebrating with the same level of joy.

King Hezekiah of Judah donated 1,000 bulls and 7,000 sheep for the people's offerings, and the officials chipped in another 1,000 bulls and 10,000 sheep. And it turned out there were plenty of consecrated priests ready to serve. The whole community of Judah, the priests, the Levites, the people who came from Israel, and even the foreigners living in Israel and Judah were all part of the joyful celebration. Jerusalem was literally bursting with joy—nothing like this had happened since King Solomon, David's son, built and dedicated the Temple.
The priests and Levites got the final word. They stood up and blessed the people. And God heard them. The sound of their prayers went all the way up to His holy home in heaven.

2 Chronicles.title: They Gave HOW MUCH?! Hezekiah's Reformation Goes Viral
paragraphs: Okay, so after the big Passover party, everyone from Israel went totally ham in all the towns in Judah. They wrecked all the weird stone statues, chopped down the creepy Asherah poles, and trashed all the local spots where people were mixing up worship with some wild stuff. They literally didn't stop until they'd hit up every corner of Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh. After that massive cleanup, they all just went back home and got back to their normal lives.

Then, King Hezekiah got all the priests and Levites sorted into crews, giving them specific jobs for the worship services. Like, who was on offering duty, and who was in charge of making sure the praise and thank-you vibes were happening whenever and wherever they worshipped God.

Hezekiah also pitched in his own stuff for the big burnt offerings—the ones they did every morning and evening, on Sabbaths, during New Moon festivals, and on all the special holy days that God's law talked about.

On top of that, he told the people in Jerusalem that it was their job to make sure the priests and Levites had everything they needed. That way, they could focus 100% on their work for God without stressing about their own stuff.

And yo, as soon as Hezekiah gave the order, the Israelites went all in. They brought the first and best of their crops—grain, new wine, oil, honey, you name it. They didn't cheap out, giving a full tenth of everything. They even brought a tenth of their cows, sheep, and anything else they had set aside for God. They piled it all up in these huge mounds. It was so much stuff that they started in the third month and didn't even finish until the seventh!

When Hezekiah and his crew saw how massive the piles of gifts were, they were like, 'Whoa!' They praised God and gave a huge shoutout to the people of Israel. Hezekiah then hit up the priests and Levites to figure out what to do with all this awesome stuff.

Azariah, the head priest from Zadok's family, was like, 'Ever since everyone started bringing all these gifts to God's Temple, we've had more than enough to eat, with tons of leftovers. God has seriously blessed his people—I mean, just look at all this!'

So Hezekiah ordered them to get some storerooms ready in the Temple. Once they were set, they moved all the offerings and sacred gifts in. A Levite named Conaniah was put in charge, with his brother Shimei as his second-in-command. A whole team of managers—Jehiel, Azaziah, Nahath, Asahel, Jerimoth, Jozabad, Eliel, Ismakiah, Mahath, and Benaiah—worked under them, following the king's and the head priest's orders. Kore, the son of Imnah, who was the guard at the East Gate, was in charge of the freewill offerings and handing out the sacred gifts. Out in the towns where the priests lived, guys like Eden, Miniamin, Jeshua, Shemaiah, Amariah, and Shecaniah were the trusted crew making sure everyone got their share. They were super fair, giving portions to all their coworkers (all the guys 30 and up) in their groups when they came to the Temple for their daily shifts. The priests were all registered by family, and the Levites (20 and older) were listed by their jobs. The official records included everyone—even their little kids, wives, and other family members. They were all so dedicated to worship, no cap. No one was left out.
The priests from Aaron's line who lived out in the country also had reliable guys who made sure every single priest and Levite on the official list got their food.

Hezekiah made sure this happened all over Judah. He was seriously the best—a good, righteous, and true leader in God's eyes. Everything he did, whether it was for the Temple worship or for following God's laws, he did it with a prayerful heart and totally crushed it. He was a huge success.

2 Chronicles.title: Hezekiah's Ultimate Trust Flex
paragraphs: Alright, so check this out. Right after Hezekiah got everything on the right track, King Sennacherib of Assyria just rolls in and starts attacking Judah. He surrounded all the fortified cities, dead-set on taking them over.

When Hezekiah realized Sennacherib was coming for Jerusalem next, he huddled up with his advisors and military leaders. Their big idea? Cut off all the water supplies outside the city. And everyone was like, 'Yeah, good call.' So a massive crew of people went out, plugged up the springs, and tore down the aqueduct. They were basically like, 'Why should the Assyrian kings show up and get free-flowing water on us?'

Hezekiah didn't stop there. He got to work fixing every broken part of the city wall, built new defensive towers, threw up another wall farther out, and beefed up the main defensive structure of the old City of David. He also mass-produced a ton of weapons—spears and shields. Then he put military officers in charge and gathered all the people in the main square by the city gate.

Hezekiah gave them a major pep talk: 'Be strong! Be brave! Don't be scared of the king of Assyria and his army. We've got more on our side than they do. He's just got a bunch of regular guys; we have our God to help us and fight for us!'
The people's morale just skyrocketed. Hezekiah's words totally fired them up.

Meanwhile, Sennacherib, who was camped out a few miles away at Lachish, sent his messengers to Jerusalem to trash-talk Hezekiah and the people of Judah. They were like, 'A message from the great King Sennacherib of Assyria: You poor saps, you think you're safe in your little 'fortress' of Jerusalem? You're sitting ducks. You think Hezekiah is gonna save you? Don't be dumb—he's feeding you a bunch of lies. When he says, 'God will save us from the king of Assyria,' he's capping. You're all gonna die. Wasn't it Hezekiah who got rid of all your local worship spots and told you there's only one place to worship? Have you even seen my track record? My ancestors and I have wrecked every country around here. Has any god ever been strong enough to stop me? Name one. Can you name a single god from any nation we've conquered that even lifted a finger against me? So what makes you think your god is any different? Don't let Hezekiah play you; don't fall for his lies. Don't trust him. No god from any kingdom has ever saved their people from me or my ancestors. What makes you think yours has a chance?'
And his messengers even added their own insults, dissing both God and God's servant, Hezekiah.

Sennacherib also kept sending letters that were super disrespectful to the God of Israel, saying stuff like, 'The gods of other nations couldn't save their people, and Hezekiah's god is no better. Probably worse.'

The messengers would go right up to the wall of Jerusalem and yell at the people on top in Hebrew, trying to scare them into giving up. They talked about the God of Jerusalem like He was just another handmade idol from some other random place.

King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah, son of Amoz, weren't having it. They started praying like crazy, calling out to heaven for help. And God answered. He sent an angel who completely wiped out the Assyrian camp—all the soldiers, leaders, and officers. Sennacherib had to go home totally humiliated, with his tail between his legs. And get this—when he went into his own god's temple, his own sons killed him.

So yeah, God saved Hezekiah and the people of Jerusalem from King Sennacherib of Assyria and from everyone else. And He kept taking good care of them. People started flooding into Jerusalem with offerings for God and expensive gifts for King Hezekiah. All the nearby nations were seriously impressed. Hezekiah's reputation went through the roof.
Sometime after that, Hezekiah got super sick, like, on his deathbed. He prayed to God, and God gave him a sign that he'd be okay.

But instead of being grateful, Hezekiah got arrogant because of the sign. This made God angry, and that anger was felt by both Judah and Jerusalem. But then Hezekiah, and the rest of Jerusalem with him, felt bad about their pride and repented. So God held back his anger for the rest of Hezekiah's life.

Hezekiah ended up crazy rich and highly respected. He built special treasuries for all his silver, gold, jewels, spices, shields, and other valuables. He had barns for his grain, new wine, and olive oil, stalls for all his different kinds of cattle, and pens for his flocks. He even started his own royal cities and had huge numbers of sheep and cattle. God made sure he was loaded. Hezekiah was also the one who rerouted the Gihon spring to bring water into the west side of the City of David. Basically, everything Hezekiah did was a success. But when the leaders of Babylon sent messengers to ask about the miraculous sign that had happened, God stepped back to see what Hezekiah would do on his own. He wanted to test what was really in his heart.

The rest of Hezekiah's story and his loyal service to God? You can read it for yourself in the 'Vision of the Prophet Isaiah son of Amoz,' which is in the official records of the kings of Judah and Israel. When Hezekiah died, they buried him in the upper section of the royal cemetery of David. Everyone in Judah and Jerusalem came to his funeral to show their respect. He was buried with great honor.
His son Manasseh became the next king.

2 Chronicles.title: From Evil King to Total Repentance: The Manasseh Story
paragraphs: So, Manasseh was only twelve when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for a wild 55 years. And let's just say God was not a fan. Like, at all. He was a straight-up evil king. He brought back all the messed-up stuff that God had cleaned out of the country before. He rebuilt all the sketchy shrines his dad, Hezekiah, had wrecked. He even set up altars for fake gods like Baal and Asherah and started worshipping stars and stuff. He even put shrines to these cosmic powers in God's own Temple, which was a huge no-no. And get this—he sacrificed his own sons. Super dark. He was into witchcraft, fortune-telling, and talking to ghosts. Basically, he made a career out of being evil, and God was seriously ticked off.

The final straw was when he put a carved statue of the goddess Asherah right in God's Temple. This was a massive slap in the face to God, who had told David and Solomon, 'This Temple in Jerusalem is where my Name will be forever.' God had promised, 'I'll never make my people leave this land, as long as they follow all the rules I gave them through Moses.'

But Manasseh totally led Judah and everyone in Jerusalem astray. They ended up doing even worse stuff than the pagan nations God had kicked out earlier. God tried to warn Manasseh and his people, but they just ghosted him.

So God sent the Assyrian army commanders after Manasseh. They put a hook in his nose, chained him up, and dragged him off to Babylon. Being in major trouble finally got his attention. He got on his knees and prayed for help, like, a full-on repentance to the God of his ancestors. And as he prayed, God was actually moved. He listened and brought him back to Jerusalem to be king again. That's when it finally clicked for Manasseh that God is the one in charge.

After that, Manasseh got to work. He rebuilt the outer wall of Jerusalem, made it higher, and beefed up the city's defenses. He also did a major spring cleaning of the Temple, throwing out all the pagan idols and the goddess statue. He got rid of all the altars he had built and dumped them outside the city. He fixed up God's altar and got the worship services going again, with proper sacrifices. He even ordered the people to worship the real God of Israel. But the people were kinda like, 'meh.' They'd say they were worshipping 'God,' but they kept going to the old pagan spots and doing the same old things.

The rest of Manasseh's story—his prayer to God, the messages the prophets gave him from God—it's all written down in the history books of the kings of Israel. His prayer, how God answered it, a whole list of his sins and all the wrong things he did, the exact spots where he built the pagan shrines and set up all the idols before he turned his life around—it's all recorded by the prophets.
When Manasseh died, they buried him in the palace garden. His son Amon became the next king.

Amon was twenty-two when he became king, and he only lasted two years in Jerusalem. In God's eyes, he was just as bad as his dad Manasseh. But here's the thing: he never repented like Manasseh did. He just kept on being evil, one bad decision after another.

In the end, Amon's own servants turned on him and assassinated him right in his own palace. Then, the people of the city went and killed the assassins. After that, they made Josiah, Amon's son, the new king.

2 Chronicles.title: This 8-Year-Old King's WILD Cleanup Mission
paragraphs: So, this kid Josiah was only eight when he got the crown. He ended up ruling for 31 years in Jerusalem. And get this—he was a genuinely good guy in God's eyes. He stayed on the right path, the one his ancestor David had laid out, without messing up once.

By the time he was sixteen—still just a teenager—he started to seriously seek the God of his ancestor David. Four years after that, in his twelfth year as king, he decided it was time for a major cleanup. He went all over Judah and Jerusalem, getting rid of all the sketchy local shrines, the Asherah poles, and all the carved or metal idols. He totally wrecked the shrines for Baal, tore down their altars, and scattered the leftover dust and ashes over the graves of the people who had worshiped them. He even burned the bones of the fake priests on their own altars. He scrubbed Judah and Jerusalem clean, inside and out. This cleanup mission spread out to the cities in Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and all the way up to Naphtali. He demolished all the altars and Asherah groves throughout Israel, crushed the idols into powder, and chopped up the local shrines for firewood. Once Israel was put back together, he went back to Jerusalem.

In the eighteenth year of his rule, after the country and the Temple had been cleaned up, King Josiah sent Shaphan, the mayor Maaseiah, and the historian Joah to fix up God's Temple. They gave all the money that the Levite guards had collected from everyone in Israel and Judah to Hilkiah the high priest. This money was then given to the project managers overseeing the work on God's Temple. They paid the carpenters, builders, and masons, and bought lumber and stone to rebuild the foundations that the previous kings of Judah had let fall apart. The workers were super honest and worked hard. Their bosses were Levites who were also amazing musicians, and they managed all the laborers and supervised everyone from job to job. Other Levites worked as accountants, managers, and security guards.

While they were handling all the money for the Temple, Hilkiah the high priest stumbled upon a copy of the Law of Moses. He told Shaphan, the royal secretary, "Yo, I just found the Book of God's Law in the Temple!" He gave the book to Shaphan, who took it to the king. Along with the book, he reported, "Everything you ordered is done. They've handed over all the money from the Temple to the managers and workers."
Then Shaphan added, "Also, Hilkiah the priest gave me this book." And Shaphan started reading it out loud to the king.

When the king heard the words from the book, God's Law, he tore his clothes in distress. He immediately called for Hilkiah, Ahikam, Abdon, Shaphan, and Asaiah and ordered them, "Go pray to God for me and for everyone left in Israel and Judah. We need to know what to do about what's written in this book. God must be seriously angry with us because our ancestors didn't follow a single thing written in this book or do any of the things we were told to do."

Hilkiah and the others went to see Huldah the prophetess. She lived in the Second Quarter of Jerusalem. They talked to her, and she told them, "This is the word from the LORD, the God of Israel: Tell the guy who sent you that God says, 'I'm about to bring disaster on this place and its people. Every single curse written in the book the king of Judah read will come true. Why? Because they've abandoned me for other gods and have made me furious with all their idol-making. My anger is burning hot against this place, and it's not going to be put out.'

"But as for the king of Judah, who sent you to ask God for guidance, tell him this is God's response to what he heard: 'Because your heart was responsive and you humbled yourself before God when you heard my words against this place and its people, and because you tore your robes and cried in front of me, I have heard you. This is God's word. I will take care of you. You will die in peace and be buried peacefully. You won't have to see the disaster I'm going to bring on this place and its people.'"
The men took her message back to the king.

The king didn't waste any time. He gathered all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem. Then he went up to the Temple of God with everyone—priests, prophets, and all the people, from the most important to the least. He read aloud the entire Book of the Covenant that was found in God's Temple. The king stood by his pillar and made a solemn promise to God to follow the covenant. He committed to following God with all his heart and soul, obeying all the commands and rules written in the book.
Then he made everyone in Jerusalem and Benjamin promise to do the same. And they did. They committed to the covenant of God, the God of their ancestors.

Josiah did a complete sweep, getting rid of all the disgusting idols throughout Israelite territory and got everyone to start fresh, serving and worshiping their God. For the rest of Josiah's life, the people stayed on the right path, faithfully following the LORD, the God of their ancestors.

2 Chronicles.title: Josiah's Last Stand: The Passover Party That Went Down in History
paragraphs: Josiah threw a massive Passover party for God in Jerusalem. On the fourteenth day of the first month, they sacrificed the Passover lambs. He gave the priests the full rundown and really hyped them up for leading the worship at God's Temple. He also told the Levites, who were in charge of teaching Israel all about worship, "Yo, put the sacred Chest in the Temple that Solomon, David's son, built. You don't have to lug it around on your shoulders anymore! Just serve God and his people, Israel. Get your families organized for your jobs, just like King David and his son Solomon wrote down."

"Alright, take your spots in the sanctuary. We need a team of Levites for every group of regular folks. Your job is to handle the Passover lambs, get yourselves ready, and prep the lambs so everyone can celebrate Passover just like God told Moses."

Josiah himself chipped in a crazy amount: 30,000 sheep, lambs, and goats, plus 3,000 bulls. Everything they needed for the Passover bash was there. His officials also pitched in for the people, the priests, and the Levites. Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel, the leaders at God's Temple, gave 2,600 lambs and 300 bulls to the priests for the Passover offerings. Conaniah and his brothers, Shemaiah and Nethanel, along with the Levite bosses Hashabiah, Jeiel, and Jozabad, donated 5,000 lambs and 500 bulls to the Levites.

Everything was set for the worship service. The priests were in their positions, and the Levites were at their posts, just like the king ordered. They sacrificed the Passover lambs, and while the priests sprinkled the blood, the Levites skinned them. Then they set aside the big burnt offering for each family group to offer to God, following the instructions in the Book of Moses. They did the same thing with the cattle. They roasted the Passover lamb just right and boiled the other holy offerings in pots and pans, and then served everyone super fast.
After everyone had eaten the holy meal, the Levites served themselves and the priests from Aaron's line. The priests were working late into the night, handling all the offerings on the altar.

The Asaph singers were all in their spots, following the instructions from David, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, the king's prophet. The security guards were at every gate, and the Levites even served them because they couldn't leave their posts.

That day, everything for the worship of God went off without a hitch. They celebrated the Passover and gave the burnt offerings on God's altar, exactly as Josiah had commanded. The Israelites kept the party going for seven days with the Feast of Unleavened Bread. No cap, the Passover hadn't been celebrated like this since the prophet Samuel's time. None of the kings had ever pulled this off. But Josiah, the priests, the Levites, all of Judah and Israel who were there, plus the people of Jerusalem—they made it happen. This legendary Passover went down in the eighteenth year of King Josiah's rule.

But then, a while later, after Josiah had fixed up the Temple and everything, King Neco of Egypt marched out to Carchemish on the Euphrates River to go to war. Josiah, for some reason, went out to fight him.

Neco sent messengers to Josiah, saying, "Dude, what's your problem with me, King of Judah? I'm not here to fight you, but the country I'm at war with. God told me to hurry, so don't get in my way. You'll just be messing with God, who's on my side, and he'll take you out."

But Josiah was just itching for a fight and wouldn't listen to a word Neco said (which was actually God talking through him). Even though King Josiah wore a disguise when they met on the plain of Megiddo, archers still shot him.
The king told his servants, "Get me out of here—I'm hit bad."

So his servants got him out of his chariot, put him in a backup chariot, and rushed him back to Jerusalem. He died there and was buried in the family cemetery. All of Judah and Jerusalem came to his funeral. The prophet Jeremiah even wrote a sad song for Josiah. That song is still sung by the choirs of Israel today. You can find it in the book of Laments.

The rest of Josiah's story, his awesome and devout life that followed God's Word, the whole thing from beginning to end, is written in the Royal Records of the Kings of Israel and Judah. After he died, the people chose his son Jehoahaz to be the next king in Jerusalem.

2 Chronicles.title: Judah's Epic Fail & Final Chapter
paragraphs: Alright, so this dude Jehoahaz was 23 when he started his rule. He was king in Jerusalem for, like, only three months. The king of Egypt came and kicked him off the throne and made the country pay him a crazy amount of money—almost four tons of silver and 75 pounds of gold.
Then Neco, the king of Egypt, made Eliakim, Jehoahaz’s brother, the new king of Judah and Jerusalem. But he changed his name to Jehoiakim. Then he dragged Jehoahaz back to Egypt with him.
Jehoiakim was 25 when he became king, and he ruled for eleven years in Jerusalem. God's take on him? He was a seriously bad dude.

Then Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon, declared war on him. He tied him up in bronze chains, planning to take him as a prisoner to Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar also jacked a bunch of stuff from God's Temple and put it in his own palace in Babylon.
The rest of the story about Jehoiakim, all the messed-up, disrespectful stuff he did and what happened to him because of it, is all written down in the history books of the kings of Israel and Judah.
His son, Jehoiachin, became the next king.

Jehoiachin was 18 when he became king. But he only lasted for three months and ten days in Jerusalem. And yeah, God thought he was a bad king, too. In the spring, King Nebuchadnezzar had him brought to Babylon, along with all the valuable stuff left in God's Temple. Then he made his uncle Zedekiah a puppet king over Judah and Jerusalem.

Zedekiah was 21 when he started as king. He ruled in Jerusalem for eleven years. As far as God was concerned, he was just another evil king. He didn't feel bad at all when the prophet Jeremiah told him what God wanted. Then he made things even worse by rebelling against King Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him promise in God's name that he'd be loyal. He got super stubborn and just wouldn't listen to God; turning back to God never even crossed his mind.

The leaders, priests, and even the regular people all started acting just as bad. It was like an epidemic of evil. They started doing all the disgusting things the other nations did and trashed God's Temple, which had just been made holy in Jerusalem.

God, the God of their ancestors, kept sending them warning messages over and over. He felt bad for his people and his Temple and wanted to give them every chance to get it right. But they just wouldn't listen. They made fun of God's messengers, hated the message, and basically treated the prophets like they were clowns. God got more and more ticked off until there was no going back. So God sent in Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon. He came and just started killing everyone, even in the Temple itself. It was a total massacre: young men, young women, old people, weak people—he didn't care, he killed them all.

And then he looted God's Temple, taking everything valuable. He cleaned it out completely, emptying the treasuries of the Temple, the king, and his officials. He hauled everyone and everything off to Babylon. He burned God's Temple to the ground, knocked down the wall of Jerusalem, and set all the buildings on fire—everything valuable was destroyed. Anyone who survived was taken as a prisoner to Babylon and became a slave to Nebuchadnezzar and his family. This whole exile and slavery thing lasted until the kingdom of Persia took over.
This was exactly what God had said would happen through the prophet Jeremiah: the empty land would finally get its long-overdue rest, a 70-year rest to make up for all the times they ignored it.

In the first year of Cyrus, the king of Persia—and this was to make God's message through Jeremiah come true—God prompted King Cyrus to make an official announcement across his whole kingdom. He wrote it down, and this is what it said: 'From Cyrus, king of Persia, a proclamation: God, the God of the heavens, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth. He has also told me to build him a Temple for worship in Jerusalem, which is in Judah. All of you who are God's people are free to go back—and may your God be with you! Let's go!'

Ezra.title: The Great Return: Rebuilding the Temple!
paragraphs: Alright, so check it. First year of King Cyrus of Persia's reign. This was wild—it was the fulfillment of what God had promised through the prophet Jeremiah. God basically gave King Cyrus a nudge, and Cyrus decided to make a huge announcement across his entire kingdom. He wrote it all down, and it went something like this:

From Cyrus, the king of Persia, a proclamation: God, the God of the heavens, has legit given me all the kingdoms of the earth. He's also tasked me with building Him a Temple in Jerusalem, which is in Judah. So, who among you is part of His crew? May God be with you! You should head to Jerusalem in Judah and build the Temple of God, the God of Israel, who is the God in Jerusalem. For anyone not going, wherever you are, you need to support the ones who are. Hook them up with silver, gold, supplies, and animals for the road, plus some freewill offerings for God's Temple in Jerusalem.

So, the leaders of the families from Judah and Benjamin, along with the priests and the Levites—basically everyone God had prompted—got ready to go build The Temple of God in Jerusalem. Their neighbors were super supportive, backing them with all sorts of stuff: silver, gold, tools, pack animals, and a bunch of expensive gifts, on top of all the other voluntary offerings.

And get this—King Cyrus also returned all the items from The Temple of God that Nebuchadnezzar had looted from Jerusalem and stuck in the temple of his own gods. Cyrus, king of Persia, put his treasurer, Mithredath, in charge of handing everything over. Mithredath made a complete inventory for Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah. Here's the list:

30 gold dishes
1,000 silver dishes
29 silver pans
30 gold bowls
410 matching silver bowls
1,000 other miscellaneous items.
All in all, it was 5,400 gold and silver items that Sheshbazzar took with him when he led the exiles from Babylon back to Jerusalem.

Ezra.title: The Ultimate Roll Call: Who Came Back from Babylon?
paragraphs: Alright, so here's the 411 on the people from the province who finally came back from captivity. These were the exiles that King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon had dragged off. They made their way back to Jerusalem and Judah, each heading to their own hometown. They rolled in with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispar, Bigvai, Rehum, and Baanah.
Here’s the breakdown of the Israelite families who returned, by their fam line:

From Parosh's crew: 2,172. From Shephatiah's: 372. From Arah's: 775. From Pahath-Moab (the descendants of Jeshua and Joab): 2,812. From Elam's: 1,254. From Zattu's: 945. From Zaccai's: 760. From Bani's: 642. From Bebai's: 623. From Azgad's: 1,222. From Adonikam's: 666. From Bigvai's: 2,056. From Adin's: 454. From Ater (Hezekiah's descendants): 98. From Bezai's: 323. From Jorah's: 112. From Hashum's: 223. From Gibbar's: 95.
